summary: The assessee was assessed to wealth tax for the assessment years 1965 66, 1966 67 and 1967 68 (the respective valuation dates being March 31, 1965, March 31, 1966 and March 31, 1967 respectively. In each of the assessments, the Wealth Tax Officer included a sum of Rs. 1,04,636/ and the assessee appealed to the Appellate Assistant Commissioner and urged that as it maintained its books of account in accordance with the cash system of accounting the accrued interest on the money lending investments could not be included in the wealth tax assessments. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner followed the "Commissioner of Wealth tax Bihar and Orissa vs Vysyaraju Badreenarayana Moorthy Raju (Orissa)(1), The Wealth Tax Officer appealed to the Tribunal and contended that accrued interest was liable to be included in wealth tax assessments of the assessee. The Tribunal rejected the contention of the assessee and held that accrued interest could not be excluded in the wealth Tax assessments of the assesee. The Revenue appealed to the Supreme Court. The question for consideration was whether the accrued interest was chargeable to wealth tax under the Wealth Tax Act, wealth tax Act, wealth Tax Officer was in law justified in including in the net wealth of the assessee interest due on accrual basis (though not realised) on the outstandings of the money lending business, the accounts of the assessee being maintained on cash basis interest due on the valuation date. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1.1 The method of accounting, mercantile or cash or hybrid, is of no relevance for the purpose of determining the assets of the assessee.[309A] 1.2 The method of valuation, mercantile or Cash or hybodrid, is a system of accounting, of mercantile or cash, is of little relevance for the purposes of determining the asset of the assessee [309D] 1.3 The method of computation of the assets of an assessee calls for a determination of his assets and debts as on the valuation dates. The method of calculation of the assets is of no significance for the purpose for determining the assets. [309E] 1.4 The method of computing the assets of a assessee under the Wealth tax Act is of no importance for the purpose o determining the assets, of the assessee,.[309F] 1.5 The method of calculating the assets of assessee is of no relevancy for the purpose Of determining the assets and debts of the assessee under the wealth tax Act. That being so, the conclusion is inescapable that even though the accounts of assessee are maintained on cash or hydrid, the value which, in the opinion of the Wealth Tax officer, the asset would fetch if sold in the open market on the valuation day. It is immaterial whether the assessee employs one system of accounting or another. [309F] 2.6 The method of determining the value of assets of an assesses under the Wealthtax Act is of little importance for the purposes o determining the asset. That being, so, the inference is inescapable that Even though the accounts are maintained on Cash basis interest due to accrual basis, though not realised, on the out standings of the moneys lending business are liable to be excluded in computing the net wealth. [309G] 2.7 The method of ascertaining the assets of every assessee under the Income Tax Act is of great importance for the determination of the assets. That being done, the conclusion becomes inescapable that even if the accounts of a assessee are maintained, on cash basis, interest due on receipt of the same is determined pursuant to sub section (I) of section 7 as the estimated price, which, in this opinion of the Income Tax Officer, the asset will fetch if sold on the valuationdate. It is apparent that what accrues as a right also falls to be included within the assets of An assessee under the Gift Tax Act.

The respondent was a workman of the Central Administrative Tribunal. He was dismissed from service on the ground that he was not a workman. The Tribunal held that the respondent was not a 'workman ' within the meaning of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947. The respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of dismissal. The High Court reversed the order of the Tribunal imposing a lesser penalty on the respondent. The High court reversed the order on the ground of absence of any evidence. The Tribunal also held that the penalty of dismissal from service imposed upon the respondent was disproportionate to the proved facts of the case. The respondent preferred an appeal before this Court. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The order of the High Court imposing a lesser punishment on the respond ent cannot, therefore, be sustained. [33F] 2. The order imposing a lesser penalties on the responde nt cannot, therefore be sustained. In the instant case, the respondent failed into t he category of a workman and the Tribunal could exercise t he powers of an industrial court for giving appropriate reli ef is unavailable in this case, since the respondent had ma de his choice of forum and was even otherwise dealt with und er the Government Servants (Conduct) Rules which are undispu tedly applicable to him. [33G] 3. The order passed by the Tribunal imposing the lesser penalty on t he respond ent cannot be sustained. The Tribunal could not interfere with the penalty if the conclusion of the Inquiry Officer or the competent authority is based on evidence even if some of it is found to be irrelevant or extraneous to the matter. [33H] 4. The High ci tution could not interfere in the penalty if t he conclusion of the Enquiry Officer or the Tribunal is based on eviden tence even if some one of it is find to be irrelevant and extraneous to the matters. [33A] 5. The High Ci t Court had no jurisdiction if the findings of the Tribunal were "unreasonable" and ordered his reinstatement in service with fu ll back wages.

The appellants were the legal representatives of the deceased plaintiff Inacio Martins who died pendente lite. He had filed a suit for a declaration and an injunction to restrain the defendants from dispossessing him from the property known as 'Palmar ' comprising seven lots of coconut grove situated at Caranzalem belonging to defendant No. 1. The suit was dismissed as the Trial Court came to the conclusion that the plaintiff was no more in possession of the property in respect of which he claimed to be a lessee. The first appellate court dismissed the suit holding that the suit was barred by the principle of res judicata in view of the dismissal of the former suit No. 157 of 1968. The High Court dismissed the suit. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the suit being barred by the principles of res judicata, the suit was not barred by Order 2 Rule 2(3) of the Code of Civil Procedure. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The question which arose in the suit was whether defendant No.1 was a tenant in respect of the land in question. If the decision of the Mamlatdar is in favour of the party raising the plea, the suit for possession would have to be dismissed, because it would not be open to the Civil Court to give any relief to the landlord by way of possession of the agricultural land. If, on the other hand, the Mamlatdar rejects the plea raised under the Tenancy Act, the Civil Court would be entitled to deal with the dispute on the footing that the defendant is a trespasser. [1032C D] 1.2 The jurisdiction of the Civil Courts stands wholly barred by virtue of Section 58(2) of the Act from settling, deciding, deciding or dealing with any question which is by or under the Act required to be settled, decided and dealt with by the Mamlatdar. [1033C D] 2.1 The jurisdiction is, therefore, vested in the Mamlatdar under Section 7 of the Act and Section 58(1) specifically bars the jurisdiction of all other courts to settle, decide or deal with any question arising which is by and under the Act require to be settled. [1034D] 2.2 The question which arises in the suit is whether defendant No1 was a trespasser. If the defendant who is sued as a trespasser raises a plea of tenancy, a question arises whether his plea of tenancy can be decided by the Civil Court as incidental to the grant of relief for possession or is the Civil Court precluded from deciding the same in view of Section 7 read Section 58(3) read Section 58 (2) of Act. [1035E] 2.3 The jurisdiction is vested in the Civil Court under Section 7 read section 58(2). The jurisdiction is therefore vested in the Collector under Section 7. The jurisdiction is also vested in the Revenue Court under Section 8 of the Act. [ 1035F] 2.4 The jurisdiction is thus vested in the revenue Court under Section7 of the Act, and Section 58 (1) specifically prohibits the jurisdiction of any other court to settle, deciding or deal with such issues which are by or under or the Act requiredto be settled, decide or dealt with by such Mamlatdar. [ 1036G] 2.5 The jurisdiction is not vested in the Tahsildar under Section 7, but Section 58( 2) specifically bars jurisdiction of all courts to settle decide or dealwith any question which was by or under Act required to been settled, decided or dealt with.

The petitioners are carpenters. They are termed as daily rated employees. In this petition under Article 32 of the Constitution, they seek enforcement of their fundamental right to have equal pay for equal work. They want the same pay of the regular employees as carpenters or in the alternative, the minimum wages prescribed by the Deputy Commissioner for like categories of workmen. The case of the Corporation is that the unit where the petition ers are working is a factory registered under the Factories Act. The Corporation has clearly stated that there are no regular employees of the petitioners ' categories in its establishment and, as such, the question of payment to the petitioners does not arise. But to avoid or minimise further loss, it is stated that the Corporation has reduced its overheads and maintained only the administrative staff in the production centers at different parts of the State and no permanent craftsmen are employed. The financial aspect of the Corporation was stated to be not encouraging, and indeed it is disappointing. But to prevent or minimise further losses, it is said that the Corporation had reduced its overhead and maintained only its administrative staff in its production centers at various parts of the country and no permanent Vishaftsmen are engaged in the construction industry. The Court, therefore, cannot direct the Corporation to apply the rates prescribed under exhibit P. 2 unless the Government makes it applicable to employees of the Corporation. [669G H; 669A] The Court, however, cannot direct, the Corporation to applied the rates prescribed by exhibit P.2 unless the Government make it applicable to employee of the Corporation.[669B] The principle of "equal pay for equal Work" is not one of the fundamental rights expressly guaranteed by our Constitution. There the Court pointed out that principle of " equal pay for Equal work" is not another of the fundamental right expressly guaranteed by the Constitution. There is no distinction between the same set of employees by the same master in the same establishment on the basis of qualifications, duties and responsibilities of the posts concerned. It is important to emphasize that equal pay for equality is a concomitant of Article 14 of the Constitution. From the averments in the pleadings of the parties it will be clear that the Corporation have no regularly employed carpenters, and craftsmen. The principal claim of the petitioners therefore fails and is rejected.

The prosecution case was that on the date of the incident, the deceased was in the company of the accused 1 and 2. The deceased was a student of the college. The deceased had a student of Class I. The deceased and the accused were friends. The deceased used to visit the college and the accused used to visit his college. The accused used to come to the college and he used to visit him. The deceased told the deceased that he would be taken to the college. On the next day, the deceased told the accused that he would take the deceased to the college but he would not take the deceased. The deceased informed the deceased that the deceased would take the appellant to the college where he would take him to the college, but the deceased told him that he would not come back. The deceased then told the deceased to take the deceased back to the college to take the appellant back to the College. The deceased thereafter told the deceased not to come back. On the same day, the appellant and the deceased went to the college along with the deceased and asked the deceased to come back to the house of the deceased. On the way, the deceased informed the appellant that he would come back to his college. On reaching the college, the deceased went back to the school and asked the appellant to come back and he would take her back to the hospital. The deceased replied that he would go back to the village and he would not go back to his house. The deceased asked the deceased not only to come back but also to take the injured to the college for taking the injured to hospital. The appellant replied that he had not come back to her house and he would go to the college on the next day. The deceased also told the deceased about the incident. The deceased stated that he would give him a statement to the police. The deceased further stated that he had told the deceased what he had told him that the deceased had told him to come back after taking the injured. The deceased gave a statement to police that he would bring the deceased back after taking him to the hospital and that he would send him to the police station. The police registered a case against the accused 1 to 4 and convicted them under section 302 read with section 34 I.P.C. and sentenced them to undergo imprisonment for life under section 302 I.P., and sentenced them. The High Court dismissed the appeal of the State. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the retracted judicial confession of accused 5 could not be relied upon against accused 6 in view of the fact that accused 6 who had been tried alongwith accused 5 had been acquitted by the High Court of the charge of conspiracy under section 302, read with section 120B I.P,C. and no appeal against their acquittal had been filed in the High Court and also the fact that the accused 5 was not a party to charge No.4 which was framed only against accused 1, 6 and 7. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The retracted judicial confession cannot be relied upon in this case in view of section 114 read with section 114 readwith section 114 read along with section 114 of the Evidence Act. [138B C] 2.1 The retracted judicial confessions of accused 5 can not be relied on against accused 6. In view of the facts that accused 6 had been acquitted, the retracted judicial confessions cannot be relied on. [138F] 2.2 The retracted judicial confessional confession of accused5 could not be acted upon against accused 5 in view of his acquittal under section 302/34 I.P..C. and the confirmation of the conviction and sentence awarded to accused 6 by the trial court under section 302.

The appellant 's father had executed a will in favour of the respondent, and the appellant 's sons had received substantial benefit under the will. The appellant 's son, who was the sole executor of the will alleged to have executed the will, was examined by the respondent. The trial court held that the appellant had not established that when Lakshmamma was alleged to have signed the will she was in a sound and disposing state of mind. The High Court, however, held that the will in question was not proved to be the last will and testament of Lakshmamma. The High court, however, took the view that the appellant ' s sons had received a substantial benefit under a will and since he had taken a leading part in its execution, the onus was heavy on him to remove the suspicions attending the execution of the document and to establish that Lakshmamma had really understood its contents, had approved of them and had put her signatures on it when she was in sound and disposing mind. The appellant appealed to this Court. HELD : (i) The High Court was in error in coming to the conclusion that it was not shown that the testatrix fully understood the contents of the will and put her signature on it when he was in a position to state the contents of his will. [446 B] (ii) The evidence of the appellant was clearly inconsistent with the appellant ' 's case about previous instructions and so it would be necessary to refer to the broad features, and dispositions of the will. [467 E] (iii) The evidence adduced by the appellant on the question of execution of the will was clearly inconsistent and inconsistent with the evidence adduced by him on the question. [467 D] (iv) The evidence led by the appellant was consistent with the appellant "s case about earlier instructions and so he would be presumed to have known the provisions of the instrument he had signed. [467 B] (v) The evidence on the question was clearly inconsistent. [467 C] (vi) The evidence was clearly inconsistent to the appellant 'S son 's case regarding previous instructions and, so it would not be difficult to treat the evidence of this witness as suffi cient to prove that the testatrix did not know the contents of her will and put his signature on it.

In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the use which is generally made of the arc carbon under consideration was duly proved to be that of production of powerful light used in projectors in cinemas. The petitioners in these petitions challenged the validity of a notification issued by the Government of Gujarat on June 26, 1985 amending the Gujarat Minor Mineral Rules 1966, hereinafter referred to as the Rules, amending the Gujarat minor Mineral Rules 1966. The petitioners in these writ petitions challenged the vires of the said notification on the ground that the said notification was in contravention of clause (b) of Article 304 of the Constitution. The petitioners contended that the said clause was violative of Article 301 of the Constitution and that the said Act was violative of article 301 of the Consti tution of India. The petitioners also contended that the impugned notification was in violation of clause (a) of Article 301 and that the impugned Notification was in contravention to clause (b). The petitioners contended (1) that the royalty levied and covered under the Rules should be applied only for mineral development and could not be used for any other purpose; (2) that the impugned Act was in contravention o clause (b), (c) and (d) of Article 300 of the Constitution; and (3) that the said impugned notification was violative of clause (c) of Article 19 of the Constitution inasmuch as it was in contravention with clause (b); and (4) that the State Government was empowered to make rules for regulating the grant of quarry leases, mining leases or other mineral concessions in re spect of minor minerals and for purposes connected therewith. Dismissing the writ petitions, ^ HELD: (1) The impugned notification was not in contravention of Clause (b) and (c) as the said clause did not authorise the State Government to show such concession while promulgating the Rules which are in the nature of subordi nate legislation is also of no consequence. [419D] (2) The impugned Notification was not in accordance with clause (c). The fact that section 15 of the Act does no authorise the State Govern ment to show such concessions while promulgating rules which are in nature of subcli nate Legislation is also of No consequence. No express power need to conferred on such subordinate authority in order to make a classification for purposes of implementing the policy of the Act under which the Rules are made. [421E] (3) The State Government is empowered to make Rules for regulating the granting of quarry leases. The rules are made for regulating the Grant of quarry leases and mining leases. [422D] (4) The State is empowered to frame rules for regulating grant of quarry lease, mining leases, mining lease or other mineral concession in re spect. Rule 18 of the Rules provides for the determination of the rate of royalty payable in respect of minor minerals. The original rule 21 was substituted by new rule 21 by the issue of impugned notification on 26 6 1985 which provides that a holder of a Parwana granted under the Rules shall pay royalty at the rate of 50 per cent of the royalty payable by the lessees and no royalty shall be charged from Nimbhadas of village Potters who manufacture upto one lakh bricks per year and by the village potters whose annual production was not exceeding two lakh bricks and who supply at least one lakh bricks to the Rural Housing Board or Panchayats. Under rule 18 of the rules the period of lease in the case of the minor minerals can be for a much longer period, it can be upto 10 years in respect of major minerals except in the case o ordinary sand, Kankar Murram and gravel a lease can be granted upto three years, and the area or land covered by a mining lease is governed by rule 15 which says that no quarry lease shall be granted for an area exceeding 10 hectares in case of specified minor mineral and 20 hec tares in the case for other minerals.

The appellant was a hereditary trustee of the temple. He was appointed as a trustee of the said temple. He took a different view and proceeded on the basis that trusteeship of the Kumaran Koil was not hereditary. The Subordinate Judge held that the appellant was a mere hereditary trustee and the suit was not barred by limitation. The High Court allowed the appeal and set aside the judgment of the Subordinate Judge. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the appellant is a hereditary trustee within the meaning of section 6(9) of the Madras Act 19 of 1951. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The appellant is a mere hereditary trustees. The fact of the transmission of the rights, estate, obligations, and charges of a deceased person to his heir or heirs does not rest upon independent title, [446 B] (2) The office of a hereditary trustee is in the nature of property. [446 C] (3) The office is in the character of property. It is not possible to say that there is a succession of As office to another when on the efflux of the period for which A was appointed, there is a vacancy and B is elected to that vacancy. [447 D] (4) The office must be transmitted to the successor according to some definite rules of descent which by their own force designate the person to succeed. [448 E] (5) The right by which one set of men may acquire a property in all the goods, movables and other chattels of a corporation. The fact that transmission of the right, estate, obligation, and charges, of a deceased man to his heir and heirs. " The office of the appellant is hereditary within the meaning Of section 6(8) of the Act. [445 E] (6) The appellant must be held to be a trustee within the ambit of section 6 (9) of Act 19 of1951. [456 F] (7) The appellant was a merely hereditary trustee within section 6(7) of Act 18 of 1951.

The respondents were the heirs and legal representatives of one Amarchand N. Shroff deceased. The Income tax Officer found that the amounts received by the heirs and the legal representatives after his death should be deemed by the fiction incorporated in sub section (1) to be income received by the deceased person before his death and that received by his heirs and legal representative after his death. The Commissioner of Income tax, Bombay City, held that the amounts were received by the legal representatives and that the amount was earned by the deceased after his death and therefore the income received by them after his death was assessable to income tax under section 24B(1) of the Income tax Act. The Commissioner, however, held that on a correct interpretation of section 24B the amounts which were received by a deceased person before the publication of the notice referred to in sub section 1 of section 22 or before he was served with a notice under sub section (2) of section 22, were liable to be assessed to income tax. The Commissioner held that on the correct interpretation of the section the amounts which are sought to be taxed and which have been held not to be liable to tax were those which were not received in the previous year and were therefore not liable to tax in the several years of assessment. The Commissioner also held that the amount received by the widow in the previous years was liable to tax under section24B(1), but in the previous previous year and which had not been assessed but would have been assessed as income received by him if death had not taken place. The Commissioner further held that the income received subsequent to the previous year in which Amarchand died was liable to be taxed as income received after his death but in the subsequent year, the income received after the death of the deceased was assessable to tax under s 24B(I) of the Act. The High Court held that on correct interpretation of s.24B the amounts received were liable to tax and that received after his lifetime should be deemed to have been received by him when the income was received had he been living. The Revenue appealed to this Court. HELD : (i) The fiction is limited to the cases provided in the three subsections of section 24 B and cannot be extended further than the liability for the income received in the earlier year. [707 B] (ii) The fiction cannot be extended beyond the object for which it was enacted. In the present case the fiction is limited only to the cases mentioned in the three sub sections of section 24A and cannot be applied further than the liabilities for the income arising in the previous assessment year. [807 C] (iii) The fiction does not extend beyond the object of which it was introduced. [808 D] (iv) The fiction can be extended beyond what is enacted. In cases covered by the two sub sections of s 24B, the legal representatives have, by fiction of law, become assessees as provided in that section but that fiction cannot be applied beyond the object. [809 E] (v) The fiction must be limited to the case provided in the two subsections of section24B and cannot be extend further than the Liability for the income derived in the previous Year. [810 E] (vi) The fiction in section 24B cannot be extended to the cases covered by sub sections 1, 2 and 3 of section 24D. [811 F] (vii) The fiction of the fiction is confined to the cases specified in the three clauses of section 24(B) and cannot be limited to cases provided in those three clauses. [812 E] (viii) The fiction introduced by section 24B is limited to those cases provided in sub sections 1 and 2 of section 24C and cannot be restricted to the cases enumerated in the three sections.

The petitioners who were members of the Andhra Pradesh Public Employment (Requirement as to Residence) Rules, 1959, were appointed either directly or by transfer to posts reserved under the Andhra Pradesh State Public Employment ( Requirement) Rules, 1960 for domiciles of Telengana region. The petitioners who were appointed either by promotion or by transfer were appointed either on promotion or by transfers to posts reserved for the members of the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes. The petitioners challenged the validity of the Rules on the ground that they were violative of article 14 of the Constitution. The petitioners contended that article 16(3) of the Constitution was ultra vires the Constitution. Held, that the power to make any law in a special case prescribing requirement as to residence in a part of a State is not absolute and is not limited to the requirement of residence in a particular part of the State. The words 'any requirement ' and 'any requirement as to resident within that State ' in article 35(a) are not intended to be used in the sense of residence in the State or Union territory. The words "any requirement ' are not intended merely to include residence in parts of the State but also to include residence within the State. It is not necessary to express any opinion whether delegation to the Central and/or State Governments to provide by rules for the further implementing of the law made by Parliament is valid or not. The words are not intended only to include residence but also to exclude residence within the state. The words must be construed in their widest sense and must be construed as comprehending the idea of residence in parts. The words of the clause are not intended as to residence within the Union territory. It is only to be remembered that the words 'any provision ' in article 16(2) are not used in the same sense as the words 'or any requirement as to domicile ' in article 15(3). The words 'or ' in article 17(3) are not meant to be used to include residence outside the State. They are not intended either to be used as residence in the Union territory or to be used for residence in the state or to be in the Union Territory. The words in article 17 (3) are intended to be construed in the sense that they are used in the wider sense and are intended to cover residence in parts in the State. If the words are used in a wider sense, the words 'and ' in article 14 must be construed to have been used in the narrower sense. The words cannot be used to enlarge the scope of the words in article 14. The words used in article 17 are not intended in the sense in which they are used. The words can be used to exclude residence in parts only. The words may be used to cover residence within the territory of the Union territory and not to include residence. The words do not mean residence in parts but only to include a residence in parts which are not intended. The words have to be construed as including residence in parts and not to exclude residence. The word 'or ' is not intended to include residence as a part of the Union Territory but also to cover residence outside the Union territory of India. The words mean residence in part only. The word "or ' is used in the wide sense of residence. The expression 'or ' has been used in a wide sense. The word is used in a broad sense and includes residence in part. The words, therefore, cannot be used in a narrow sense. The expression "or ' has to be construed to mean residence in a State or Union Territory. It is difficult to think that the Constituent Assembly was thinking of residence in Districts, Taluqas, cities, towns or villages.

The appellant was tried for offences under section 52 of the Indian Post Office Act, 1898 and in two of them, also for offences under sections 467 and 471 of the Indian Penal Code. The Additional Sessions judge convicted the appellant and sentenced him to rigorous imprisonment for three years and to pay a fine of Rs. 500/ . The High Court dismissed the appeal of the appellant. In appeal to this Court, it was contended that the prosecution having merely shown that the registered letters were recovered from an almirah in the house in which the appellant lives the appellant, the appellant cannot be said to have secreted the letter just because it was found in the almirah which was said to have been in his exclusive possession. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: (1) The prosecution having failed to prove that these letters were in the exclusive possession of the appellant, these articles were in his exclusive custody. [413 D] (2) The prosecution has failed to prove the case. The prosecution has not been able to prove that the letters were recovered in the almirah. [413 E] (3) The prosecution had failed to prove this. [413 G] (4) The prosecution was able to prove the charge. [413 F] (5) The prosecution failed to prove. the case. [413 C] (6) The prosecution, having failed to establish that these letters had been recovered from an open almirah in the room in which the deceased lives the appellant could have been convicted under section 52 without the Court having to consider whether he had secreted the articles. [413 B] (7) The prosecution did not prove that these were in the joint possession of the deceased. [413 A] (8) The prosecution could not prove that the almirah contained, apart from the registered letters in question, certain other articles belonging to the appellant cannot sustain an inference that the almirah was even in the appellant 's joint possession along with his father because he had the opportunity to get at the articles and then infer that he must have utilized the opportunity and was therefore in their exclusive possession would be arguing in a circle. [413 H] (9) The prosecution must have failed to prove, that these letters are in the exclusive custody of the appellant and his father because they were found in the room which was said by the articles. The prosecution had not been able, to prove that they were found with the appellant. [413F] (10) The prosecution evidence was not that it was ever with the appellant it would not be legitimate to infer that the almirah had been even in the possession of the respondent. [413G] (11) The prosecution also failed to prove in the present case that these letters contained a large number of articles belonging to him. [413C] (12) The prosecution case was that these letters did not contain the articles belonging to his father. [413D] (13) The prosecution proved that these letters belonged to the father and there was no evidence that it was never with the appellant ''s father. [414F] (14) The prosecution 's case was that the appellant had an opportunity to procure the articles. It was not proved that these were found in his exclusive exclusive possession along with the appellant and their father. [466G] (15) The prosecution succeeded in proving that these letters related to the appellant ' 's possession exclusively or even jointly with his father. The prosecution failed in proving that the almirah were in the appellant's exclusive possession alongwith his father. No presumption can, therefore, be drawn against him that he had secreting them from the mere fact that they were not found in the appellant "s joint possession together with his father, because he had an opportunity of getting at the articles.

The appellants were convicted of contempt of court and sentenced to pay a fine of Rs. 1,000/ and further ordered that in case of default they shall undergo simple imprisonment for two weeks. The High Court held that the Nyaya Panchayat had no jurisdiction to pass an order staying the proceedings pending before the Nyaya Panchayat. The High court held that the order of stay passed by it staying proceedings pending before it was not proper because it did not fully evidence the fact that the High Court had passed an order staying proceedings before the Nyaya panchayat. The High ' Court also held that the application was not made before the Nyaya Sabha. The High, Court held that "the Nyaya Panchayat had not passed an order of stay of proceedings pending before a Nyaya Panchayat". The High Court also held in favour of the appellants. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the Nyaya Panchayats exercised judicial powers and, even if the Panchas erred in not staying proceedings before finding them guilty of contempt of Court it should be definitely proved that the order was passed deliberately to by pass the order of the High Court. HELD : (i) The High Court did not appreciate that the so called affidavit which was filed before the Panchas was in fact not an affidavit at all. It was no part of the duty of the Panchas to enquire from the S.D.M. about the filing of the application before him. It was not necessary that the Nyaya panchayat should enquire from the s.D. M. about the filling of the application by the s. D.M. or a certified copy of the order. [119 E F] (ii) The High court did not appreciate the evidence, but, with respect, it seems to us that the socalled affidavit which was produced before the Pancha was in fact an affidavit at the time of filing the application before the Nyaya Panchayats. It was also not necessary that a judicial officer should do so and if he bona fide does not in his discretion adjourn proceedings, it cannot be said that he has committed contempt of court. [119 F G] (iii) The High 'Court did not appreciate in the principles of law which we have mentioned above. [119 G] (iv) The High Courts did not appreciate, that the so-called affidavit which had been filed before the Panchayat was in fact a document at all. it had not been sworn to before any person authorised to administer oaths. It was only a copy of the telegram was not attached to the application. [119 A B] (v) The High, while dealing with the evidence, has not kept in mind the principles which we have set out above.

In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) The High Court erred in rejecting the statement of Ujagar Singh about the appellant ' s confessing to him that he had murdered Sheo Kishore and that sword was handed over by the appellant himself to the Police Officer at the Police Station. The evidence of the prosecution consisted of the evidence relating to motive, to his extra judicial confession to one Ujagar Singh, P.W. 2, who states that the Sub Inspector was not present when Ujagar Singh related to them the fact which had taken place at night and by Bishram Singh, P P.W 13, who 210 deposed that Ujagar Singh stated that he had come after committing the murder of the deceased. The evidence relating to the appellant ' to Ujagar Singh, fully established that the appellant did commit the murder of his deceased brother. W. 2 and that the appellant was taking his bath at night in the Canal Distributory and had said that he had then proceeded towards the police station. The evidence that the SubInspector was not present was not sufficient to establish conclusively that the person who had murdered Sheo Kumar had committed the murder of a person with whom he had enmity, had committed the offence. [208 E F] (2) The evidence of Paley singh, P.Ws. 2 and 3, who were the eye witnesses, was not sufficient for establishing conclusively that the appellant committed the murder. The evidence was not sufficient, to establish conclusively, that the person whom the appellant had committed the crime was likely to be feeling so justified in his conduct as to openly admit it to the first person he met and to go to the Police Station and report about it. [208 G H] (3) The evidence relating the appellant 'to Ujagar Singh, was corroborated by the medical evidence. The evidence showed that the appellant and his brother were sleeping in their field on account of the crops being not very high. The evidence also showed that the Sub Inspectors were not present when the Sub Inspector reached the Police Station, and the appellant 'S confession to Ujagar singh, fully established. The evidence, therefore, was not enough to establish conclusively the guilt of the appellant. [208 B C] (4) The extra judicial confession of the appellant to Ujagar Singh was not admissible in evidence as it was not admissible. The evidence in the present case was not sufficient. to establish conclusively as to conclusively that the accused had murdered Sheo Kr. Singh. The evidence did not show that the appellant should have made a statement that he had killed Sheo Kr. and was, thereafter, having a bath. It was not unlikely that the appellant could have made a confession that he had committed the murders of Sheo Sahai and was, therefore, thereafter, had gone to the Police station and report about the same. [208 C E] (5) The evidence in this case was not enough. to establish the guilt of appellant.

The appellants were elected as members of the Madhya Pradesh Munici 493 pal Corporation (Preparation, Revision and Publication of Electoral Rolls and Selection of Councillors) Rules, 1963. The appellants challenged the validity of the electoral roll on the ground that the entire election process had become vitiated on account of the defect in the notice issued under Rule 4(1) of the Rules notifying that claims and objections should be preferred within a period of 20 days from the date of publication of the notice. The appellants filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of their electoral roll on various grounds. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The writ petition was rightly dismissed by the High Court as there was no satisfactory explanation for the delay in filing the writ petition till December 28, 1978. [417C] 2. The writ Petition itself was presented on December 28,1978. The writ petitioners were entitled to the issuance of the writ. [421B] 5. The writ petitions were rightly dismissed by this Court as there were no satisfactory explanation. [422C] 6. The writ appeal is accordingly dismissed.

The complaint was dismissed by the Magistrate on the ground that the company and the directors could not rely upon their failure to call the general meeting as a defence to the prosecution. The High Court, however, held that if no balance sheet is laid before a general body, there can be no question of that balance sheet not being adopted nor of complying with the requirements of section 220 and though wilful omission to call a general body meeting and to lay the balance sheet and profit and loss account before it may expose the person responsible to punishment under other provisions of the Act, it certainly does not make him liable under the provisions of section 134(4) of the Act. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The principle laid down in Park vs Lawton(8) was applied and it was held that no offence was committed by the directors in this case under section 134 of the Companies (Amendment) Act, 1967. [435 C] (2) The principle and authority it should be held that no charge was committed by directors in this matter under section 134(1) (3) of the Old Companies Act or section 220 of the Act as the case may be, while wilful omission to calling a general body Meeting and omit to lay the Balance sheet and profit account before it might expose the person liable under other provisions Of the Act, the section does not make it obligatory. But section 134 lays down that after balance sheet and profits and loss account or the income and expenditure account, as the case might be, have been laid before a special general body, the company and their directors could not be proceeded against under section 134 (4) of that Act as the matter may be, when the requirements of sub section (2) of section 134 of that Act have not been complied with even then, the persons concerned would be liable for punishment for that default. [436 D] (3) The principle of law laid down in the Park vs Lawley(8) is not applicable to the facts of the present case. [437 C] (4) The principle that no copies of the balance sheet or profit and loss accounts before an annual general meeting is a condition precedent to the requirement that copies of such documents so laid should be filed before the Registrar. [438 F] (5) The fact that section 26 makes the offence a continuing one also shows that the obligation to file a copy of the balancesheet and profit and losses account before it is laid, is independent of the holding of a general meeting. But section 135 lays down that if the balance sheet is not adopted at the general meeting before which it is laid the general meeting, a statement of that fact and of the reasons therefore have to be annexed to the balance sheet, and to the copies thereof required to be filed with the Registrar. If no balance sheet was laid before a company at the general general meeting before the company is laid, a statement that the balance sheet was not adopted nor of compliance with the requirements Of the sub section (1) of section 220 of that section.

The appellant was convicted under section 5(1) of the West Bengal Special Courts Act, 1952, and sentenced to rigorous imprisonment for three years. The High Court dismissed the appeal. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the principle of classification upon which the differences have been made between cases and offences triable by the Special Court and those by ordinary courts is indicated in the preamble to the Act which runs as follows: "Whereas it is expedient to provide for the speedier trial of certain offences; and it is necessary to ascertain whether it is actually based on such a classification. It may be noted in this connection that in the present case the High Court has ' held the provision of section 5(I) of the Act to be ultra vires the Constitution only so far as it relates to the State Government to direct a case to be tried by a Special Court according to the special procedure provided by it for the spei cial court. Held, that the Special Court had no jurisdiction to try these "cases" of the respondents. The Special Court had jurisdiction to try the "cases" and the Special Court was not competent to try them. The Special Courts were competent to try these cases. The Special courts were competent to deal with the cases of the respondents and the Special Courts were not competent to deal them with them. The Act was not a general law and the special courts were competent under the Act to try them and to try them in accordance with the procedure prescribed by it for them. The provisions of the Act were not discriminatory in so far as they purported to vest in the State Government an absolute and arbitrary power to refer to a special court for trial such offences or classes of cases as may, in its opinion, require speedier trials.

The appellant was appointed as a Radiologist in the Maulana Azad Medical College and treated as an Associate Professor of Radiotherapy in Maulana Azad medical College. The appellant was appointed on the post of Radiologist in a teaching hospital belonging to the Central Health Service (Amendment) Rules, 1966. The appellant, who was a Radiologist, was appointed as Radiologist in that College. The respondent, who was working as a Radiographer, was appointed on a temporary basis in the said College. The post of Radiographer was later on re appointment in the Medical College. The Government of India, Ministry of Health and Family Planning, Department of Health by its letter dated February 23, 1974 informed the Delhi Administration that the appellant could not be considered for appointment to the post of Associate Professor of radiotherapy in the Ma�ulana Azad Medical college inasmuch as he did not possess at least five years ' teaching experience as Reader/Assistant Professor in the concerned speciality as required under the Central Health Services (Amendment) Act, 1966. In the meanwhile, the appellant was appointed to the post in the Medical Colleges. The appellant continued to hold the post of radiologist in the said college. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the appointment of the appellant as Radiologist. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the designation of the appellant was akin to that of honorary Professor or Associate Professor in the Hospital and that the appellant who was a radiologist in a research institution attached to the Maulana Safdarjang Hospital could not be appointed by direct recruitment as Professor of Radiology under r. (2) of the Central Health service (Amendment) rules, 1966. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The designation of the Appellant as a Radiology cum Associate Professor of Surgery (ex officio) by the University of Delhi does not give him a right to hold the Post of Associate Professor in Maulana Ansari Medical College. [804B] 2. The designation, of the appellant, as a Radiological cum Associate Professor, of Radiotherap in Maulana Safdarji Medical College, is akin to that as honorary Professor or Assistant Professor in the Willing don Hospital or the Safdarjang hospital and the mere designation of the appellants as such does not give them a right to holding the post of Assistant Professor of Radiological in Maulana Ali Medical College. By parity of reasoning, it is urged that the designation, of appellant as a Radiist cum Associate Professor in Radiotherapy cannot prevail. [805C D] 3. The designation and the status of the appellant is similar to that of Honorary Professor or Associate professor in the Willaling don Hospital or Safdarjangospital and the mere nomenclature of the appellant does not give his right to hold that the post of Professor of Radiography cannot prevail. The contention that the status of Associate Professor or Radiology cannot prevail. It is also urged that the status, of Associate Professor (ex officio), which the appellant enjoys as Radiologist cum Associate Professor or Associate Professors in the Willingsing don Hospital, cannot prevail. In the Health Ministry, holding that the teaching experience gained by the appellant as radiologist cum Associate Professors of Radiothe Surgery (exofficio) with effect from October 9, 1964 cannot be taken into consideration. [806E F] 4. The Ministry of Health cannot be heard to say that the appellant has not acquired the status of an Associate Professor orAssociate Professor of Radiologist with effect from November 9, 1964, particularly when the Central Government have been utilizing his services as such for teaching the post graduate and under graduate students of the Maulana Ansari medical College for the M.D., M.S., D.M.R.T.

The workmen of Orient Paper Mills Ltd., Brajrajnagar, have come up in this appeal by special leave against an award of the Industrial Tribunal, Orissa. The first and the main point argued was that the Tribunal was wrong in fixing the minimum wage in the Company on the basis of the average minimum wage prevailing in other industries in that region which could be compared with the Company in which minimum wages were higher than the minimum wages paid by the Company, but failed to fix the minimum wages in the award in accordance with the minimum wages being paid in those industries. Held, that the Tribunal committed no error of law in fixing the Minimum wage in the company on the basis that the minimum wage was a consolidated wage consisting of basic wages and dearness allowance, and that, in the instant case, the Tribunal committed any error of law, requiring interference by the High Court in basing its decision on the principle contained in the earlier Agreement of 1959. The Tribunal was expected to decide the dispute only as referred to it and, at the time of reference, there was not and there could possibly not be a claim for higher bonus on the basis Of the application of the Full Bench Formula. The Tribunal, in giving its decision, kept this principle in view, but came to the finding of fact that there were no other concerns in the same line of business as the Company in the region which could he compared with the company in the region. The Tribunal did not commit any error of fact, requiring interference. The Tribunal committed no mistake of law, directing the Tribunal to fix the Minimum wage.

The appellant, a Hindu widow, filed a suit for partition of the coparcenary property in the Court of the Civil Judge, Bombay, on the ground that the suit properties belonged to the joint family, that there was no prior partition and that the plaintiff was entitled to a 7/24th share. The trial court decreed the suit. The High Court dismissed the appeal. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the suit property belonged to the Joint Hindu Family and that there was a prior partition and the plaintiff was not entitled to a share in the interest which her husband had at the time of his death in the coparcenary property. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD : (1) The heirs will get his or her share in the coparcenary properties at the time when his death, a partition of the joint property was effected between him and other members of the coparcenary. [799 C] (2) The heirs would get his or their share in the share which he or she received or must be deemed to have received in the notional partition. [701 D] (3) The heirs are entitled to the share in the property which the deceased bad in the coparcenary. The heirs will have to take equally, each having one share in the deceased 's property under section 10 read with Rules 1 and 2 of that section. [702 E] (4) The heirs have to take the share in their interest which the deceased had in the coparcenary Property at the time the death. [703 E] (5) The heirs can get his orher share in the interests which the deceased has in the coparcenary estate at the time he dies. [704 F] (6) The heirs cannot get their or her share. [705 B] (7) The heirs must take the share of the deceased in the interest of which the deceased was entitled at the time his death.

The petitioner was a registered dealer under the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, and was assessed to income tax for the assessment year 1947 55. The petitioner challenged the validity of the Act on the ground that the provisions of the Act were void from the date of the commencement of the Constitution of India by reason of article 14 of the Constitution. The petitioner contended that the provisions Of the Act were not void from the commencement of Constitution of India and that in any case the procedure prescribed by the Act was a good substitute for that prescribed by the Indian Income Tax Act. Held, that the provisions in the Act were valid and the petitioner was not entitled to the relief prayed for. The provisions of the Indian Incometax Act, 1922 were not void on the ground of violation of article 20(3) of the Constitution and the provisions of article 20 of the Constitution were void. The provisions Of the Indian Income. tax Act, 1961, were not void because the petitioner was a dealer in agricultural land and was not a registered dealer. The provisions in the Indian Income Act, 1922 and the Indian Income ' tax Act, were not invalid because the petitioner had not been given discriminatory treatment even from those whose cases were referred to under section 5(1) of the Act. The provisions were not void as the petitioner was given discriminatory treatment. The provisions contained in section 5(4) of the Indian Incometax Act, 1922 are not void because they were inconsistent with the provisions of articles 20(3), (4) and (6) of the constitution. The appellant, a "commercial establishment" carried on in the premises in question, was a "commercial Establishment" within the meaning of section 2(5) of the Delhi Shops and Establishments Act, 1954. The appellant, a member of the Federation, was a member of that Association. The Federation, was formed for the purpose of carrying on the business of the Federation. The appellant was a member and was registered under the Delhi Shops & Establishments Act, 1958. The Federation was formed for carrying on the activities of the Federation and was registered as a "commercial establishments" under the Act. The Federation had its registered office in Delhi. The appellant 's name was registered as an "commercial establishment". The Federation was registered as the "commercial establishment " under the Act and was registered in Delhi. It was contended on behalf of the Federation that the activities of a Federation carried on in these premises amounted to "work in connection with, or incidental or ancillary" to trade or business in general within the latter part of the definition of "commercial establishment", and that the activities carried on in those premises amounted to a "work in relation to, or incidental and ancillary" to the trade or business of trade or business. Held, that the activity of the Federation amounts to the carrying on of any business or trade. The activity of the appellant was not "a business or trade" because by the Memorandum of Association, Articles of Association and other material, which was more or less the same, as in the present case, it was held that the activity carried on in that premises was a business or trade, and not a "commercial activity" within the definition of the expression "commercial establishment." The mere word "trade" does not necessarily mean something by which a profit is made. It will bear repetition that the Federation also publishes periodicals, bulletins etc. and issues the same to member free of this Court in R. K. Of course, that profit is ploughed back for the purposes of the Federation as set out in its Memorandum of Association. The fact of the matter is that the Federation itself publishes periodical returns, bulletins, etc. and issue the same to members free of this court in R.K. Of course that profit is Ploughedback for the purposes Of the Federation as sets out in its memorandum of Association, and is not distributed among its members.

The assessee was a Hindu undivided family headed by one Sri Trivikram Narain Singh who was a descendant of one Sri Babu Ausan Singh who was the original founder and owner of what is known as Ausanganj State in the district of Benaras. The Income tax Officer held that it was a regular annual income of the assessee and did not fall within the category of agricultural income tax. He held that it did not fall under the category of Agricultural Income tax. He observed that "in fact this income arose from a statutory obligation of the Government to pay it and though the Government recouped this from the person with whom the land was settled, land in the genealogical tree of Malikana appears in the second degree, its immediate and effective source is the Government 's statutory obligation to pay it, and this obligation is not land within the meaning of section 4(3)(viii) of the Income tax Act. The Appellate Tribunal held that the income of the trust appropriated by the assessee as remuneration during the previous year of the assessment year 1949 50 was revenue income liable to tax under the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. The High Court held that from the language of the letter and the letter of July 7, 1837, Babu Har Narain Singh and his successors were granted in perpetuity a right to one fourth of the land revenue collections itself and not merely a right to receive u sum of money calculated on that basis. The High court further held that the right which was conferred by the letter of 7th July, 1837 was a right to a share of one fourth in the net land revenue collections after deducting costs of Tahsil establishment. The High ' Court further held that "the income of the Trust appropriated by the appellant as remuneration is not received by him as rent or revenue of land; the character of the income appropriated as remuneration due is again not the same as the character in which it was received by the appellant. The High, Court held that the receipt of the assessee was agricultural income within the meaning Of section 4(4)(viii) Of the Indian Income Tax Act, 1922 and did not come within the category Of agricultural income tax as defined in the Act. The High. Court further held, that the right conferred by the letters of July 7 1837, and July 7,1837, Babu Ausha Singh and his predecessors were granted in absolute perpetuity a right of one fourth of land revenue collections themselves and not merely an right to receive rent or revenue. The High Courts further held that since the income of Sri Trivikaram Narain Singh and their successors were granted to them in perpetuity a rights to one fourth was created in favour of the assessee as his remuneration, and that the income was not agricultural income within section 4(2)(viii)of the Income tax. Act, 1922, the assessee was not entitled to the allowance. The question referred by the Appellate Tribunal was as to whether on a true interpretation of the letter of June 7, 1838, Babu Har Narayan Singh and his successor were granted in assigns a right to the share of one third in the net lands revenue collections after deduction of costs of Tahsil establishments. The High High Court held, that from the plain language of the letters of June 7 and 1837, it was manifest that the right to the land revenue was granted to the assessee. The High Curt held that from that language of the said letter, it was clear that the right of the respondent did not acquire the character of an interest in land or in land revenue. The income of the respondent was agricultural income and not exempt from taxation as agricultural income. The High courts held that the allowance varied from year to year, the source of the income still remains the arrangement and not land. The High appeals to this Court were dismissed.

The respondent purchased a business in the name of M/s. Ram Reddy, a dealer in the business of sale of certain goods. The respondent sold the goods to the appellant on the ground that the goods were purchased by him from M/s Ram Reddy, who was the dealer in the said business. The appellant contended that the respondent was not liable to pay sales tax due from the dealer in respect of the sales effected by the respondent. The respondent contended that the sales were effected by the appellant in the course of the business of the respondent and that the sales effected were in the course Of the business of M/S Ram Reddy and that the sale was not liable for sales tax due. Held, that the respondent undertook to pay the arrears of sales tax due by the transferor to the transferor and the transferee on the date of default. The respondent undertook to make payment of the arrears of tax due by him to the transferor. The respondent did not discharge the liabilities in regard to arrears of sales Tax due by the transferee. The respondent was not entitled to recover the arrears of Sales Tax due by him. The respondent had undertaken to pay the dues of sales tax and it was open to sales tax authorities to proceed against the assets of the business for realising the amount of sales tax. The respondent could not be said to be liable to pay the sales tax due on the sales effected in the course. of the business. The respondent, therefore, was not liable under section 19(2)(c) of the Act.

The appellant was a public servant. He was dismissed from service on the ground that it contravened the provisions of article 311(2) of the Constitution. The High Court held that there had been a breach of article 311 of the Constitution as, according to it, there was no duty to supply a copy of the report of the enquiry held against the appellant. The State appealed to this Court. HELD : (i) The High Court erred in holding that there had not been a breach on the part of the competent authority to provide the appellant with a copy of his report of the Enquiry Officer. The State of Gujarat will bear its own costs in this appeal. [922 D] (ii) The High court erred in holding the liability in respect of arrears of salary earned by a public servant for the period that he was actually in office. [923 E] (iii) The High ' Court erred in fastening the liability in favour of the State of Maharashtra. The State will bear its costs in this Court. [924 F] (iv) The decree of the High Court decreeing payment of arrears of pay is truly a liability in proceedings relating to a contract within section 60(2)(a) of the Act rather than under section 61. [925 B] (v) The decree in the suit of the High court decreeing payment of arrear of salary is truly a decree in proceedings relating " a contract within the meaning of section 60 of the Act.

[447 E] (3) The High, Court was right, in holding that section 48 of the Indian Mines Act and the Rules and Regulations made thereunder the respondents could request the mining authorities to exempt them from the operation of rule 76 of the Indian Coal Mines Regulation, 1946, and if exemption was granted, they could remove the coal left by the appellant in the encroached area. The appellant was a crosscutter. The appellant was suspended by the Secretary and others. The appellant challenged the order of suspension before the Industrial Tribunal. The Industrial Tribunal held that the appellant had intended to take disciplinary action against the workman but subsequently departmental proceedings were dropped and action was taken under r. 18(a) of the Standing Orders without holding any departmental inquiry and the order was communicated to the appellant. The Tribunal held that there was no misconduct and therefore the action taken under r, 18(a), was bona fide and was not colourable. The appellant appealed to this Court. HELD: (i) The Industrial Tribunal had the right to inquire into the causes that might have led to termination of service under a rule like 18(a). The Industrial Tribunal was therefore right in holding that the exercise of the power was colourable and it cannot be said that the view taken by the Industrial Tribunal was incorrect. [29 E] (ii) The Industrial Court had the right of inquire into the cause that might have lead to termination of the service under r.18(a) and if it is satisfied that the action taken was a colourable exercise of the powers or as a result of victimisation or unfair labour practice it would have jurisdiction to intervene and set aside such termination. [30 E] (iii) The Industrial Tribunals in the present case had the right under r. 19(a) to the appellant to inquire into causes that might had led to termination. [31 E] (iv) The Industrial Courts in the present cases had the right, to inquire into and decide the causes that may have led to the termination of service even under a rule similar to r. 18 (a) and (b) of the standing orders in this case. [32 D] (v) The Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, was a piece of legislation and the Industrial Disputes Act was a piece with the object of providing for the speedy disposal of industrial disputes. The Industrial Tribunals had the right in enquiring into the causes which might have led a termination of service and had taken action under r. 17 (a) by leading evidence before the tribunal to show that there was in fact misconduct and therefore, the action taken against the appellant and action taken under that rule was bona fide.

HELD : (i) The question whether the legal relationship arising out of the agreement dated October 27, 1954 was in the nature of a lease or of other character had to be decided at the trial and the previous judgment being a judgment by consent, 'could not operate as res judicata. [446 B] (ii) The question of res judicata is a mixed question of fact and law and the question whether the suit was decided or not is a mixed one. [447 C] (iii) The question is whether in fact the subordinate Court has decided the question of resjudicata. [448 C] (iv) The question as to whether the legal relations arising out of a document dated November 28, 1954, were in the nature or of a lease had to be determined at the trial. [445 E] (vi) The question, whether the legal relation arising out of an agreement dated December 28, 1954 was a case decided within the meaning of section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure, was not decided in Major section Khanna section Khanna. The High court has recorded a finding that the agreement was of the nature of an agreement. (x) The question had already been concluded by the consent decree in suit No. 150 of 1960. [437 E] (xi) The question regarding res judicata was a mixed question. The question whether in fact a document of November 27, 1955 created a lease or a lease of other character did not arise. [434 G] (xii) The question about res judicata was not a decision of the Court, and that the consent decree operates as res judicata, for it was not a judgment of the Court. [435 G] (xiii) The question relating to res judicata was one of fact and it was not decided by the Court. [404 C] (xiv) The question referred to in the plaint in the present suit was whether the rights granted were in the ownership of Filmavall Causes to exhibits motion pictures, in the theatre, under the agreement of November 27. The question was not whether it related to a matter to be decided by the court and on which the opinion of witnesses was irrelevant.

The appellant was acquitted by the Additional Sessions judge, Chittoor of an offence under section 302 Indian Penal Code. The High courts were right in holding that the discrepancies on the basis that the Trial Court rejected the evidence of all the prosecution witnesses were of a major character and that the contradictions noticed by the learned trial judge were of a serious nature. [368B] 2. The High 'Court was well justified in commenting that the discrepancies in the evidence of prosecution witnesses on account of which the Trial Court dismissed the evidence of these witnesses were of minor character and the High Court should not interfere with the order of acquittal merely because another view is also possible. [368C] 3. The High "Court was well within its jurisdiction in dealing with the evidence of a prosecution witness. The High `Court was well versed in dealing with an appeal against acquittal. [368D] 4. The HighCourt was right in observing that the discrepancies found by the Sessions Court were of a trivial character and that it had been rightly rejected by the High Court. [368E] 5. Court was well within the jurisdiction in dealing an appeal against an acquittal. [369B] 7. The High High Court was well vigh justified in commenting on the evidence on the basis Of this statement of PW 1. The evidence of the defence witnesses on the record was sufficient to sustain the conviction of the appellant under section 302 I.P.C.

The appellant was a Judge of the Supreme Court and was holding the post of Chief Justice of the High Court. He was convicted by the Chief Justice of India under section 5(1)(c) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. He was sentenced to rigorous imprisonment for a period of six months and to pay a fine of Rs. 500/ . The Chief Justice of Madras High Court, in appeal, set aside the conviction and sentence and directed the Chief Justice to take cognizance of the offence under section 5 of the Act. The Chief Justice, however, directed the Chief Judge to take cognizance in accordance with the procedure prescribed in Article 124(4) of the Constitution. The Chief Judge, however, did not take cognizance of an offence punishable under section 5. The Chief Judicial Magistrate, however, took cognizance of the offences under section 5 and directed the matter to be placed before the Chief Justice for appropriate orders. The Chief Chief Justice, in revision, set aside his conviction and sentence. The Chief Minister of Madras, filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the order of the Chief Judicial Magistrate. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. The Chief Secretary, who was the Chief Secretary of the State, filed a petition in the Supreme Court challenging the order of his Chief Judicial Magistrate and the High Court dismissed it. The Chief Ministers of Madras and Madras High Courts filed a writ Petition in the High court challenging the validity and legality of the order passed by the Chief Judicial Magistrates. The High court dismissed the writ Petition. The Chief Justices of Madras and Kerala High Courts filed appeals before this Court. The High Courts dismissed the writ petitions. The Chief Judges of Madras and Tamil Nadu High Courts filed writ petitions in the High Courts challenging the validity, legality and validity of the orders of the Chief judicial Magistrates. The Chief Secretaries of Madras and Andhra Pradesh High Courts filed petitions in the Supreme Courts challenging the vires of the Act and the validity of those orders. The High courts dismissed the writ Petitions. The Chief judicial Magistrates filed appeals before the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeals. The Chief judges of Madras and Karnataka High Courts filed special leave petitions in this Court challenging the vires and validity of those decisions. The Supreme Courts dismissed the appeals and dismissed the writ appeals. The Supreme court dismissed the appeals, holding that the Chief Judicial Judges were the authority competent to appoint and to remove a Judge from his office. The Chief executive Judges filed writ petitions challenging the vires, validity and legality. The Supreme courts dismissed the appeals on the ground that the Chief judicial Judges were the competent authority to appoint and remove a Judge. The Supreme Judges filed special leave petition in this Court. Allowing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. The Chief Law Judges are the authority competent under Article 124(5) of the constitution for removal of the Judge. The incumbent of the office of Chief Justice exercises only moral authority over his colleagues in the Supreme court and the High Courts, which has no legal sanction behind it making it justiciable. [216C D] 2. The incumbent, of the office, exercises only moral control over his colleagues, in the Supreme courts and the High courts, which has nothing to do with the functioning of the Supreme Courts. [216D E] 3. The incumbent is the office of the Chief Justice exercising only moral authority, over his colleagues. [216E] 4. The incumbent that the office of a Chief Justice of a High Court or the Supreme Court is not a vertical superior of any of them, there being no such vertical hierarchy and the Chief Justice Of India having no legal sanction over it making it obligatory. [216F] 5.

The appellant was a member of the Saha caste and was a member. The respondent was a member in the Saha caste. The appellant was a Sunri by caste but was excluded from the Scheduled Caste group because he belonged to a smaller caste group of Sunirs known as Sahas. The appellant 's case was that the respondent belonged to a larger caste group of a Sunri caste and not a member of any Schedule Caste. The Election Tribunal held that the appellant belonged to the Saha caste, a fact which appeared to have been admitted by the respondent and, therefore, did not belong to the Scheduled Caste specified in item 40. The High Court held that the Sahas were originally a smaller caste and were for that reason not a member. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the appellant was a " Sunri" by caste but he was excluded from that caste because he belonged only to a smaller community group of Sunris who bore the surname Saha. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The word "include" in the item must, without more, also refer to a caste group within the Sunri caste. [392 D] (2) The word 'include ' includes 'a caste group '. [392 E] (3) The word includes 'a person '. [391 D] (4) The word is not used in the sense in which it is used in the context in which it occurs. [392 G] (5) The word means 'include a caste group. [392 F] (6) The word does not include a caste group or a group of a group of persons. [392 C] (7) The word has not been used in the wider sense in which the word is used in a wider sense. It is not very clear whether the word 'includes a caste group called Sahas. [392 A] (8) The word, in the item referred to a caste groups within the Sunari caste, is used in wider sense. [392 B] (9) The word in the item refers to men of the Sunri Caste but not those within that caste who formed the smaller caste group. The word 'includes 'means a caste group of persons and includes a person who is a member of a Scheduled Caste. [392 H] (10) The word cannot be used in the restricted sense in which a caste group is used in its wider sense. The word includes a caste group as a group of individuals. [392F] (11) The word may include a caste or a group. [391 C] (12) The word must, without any more, also, refer to a Caste group. [393 C] (13) The word include a caste. [393 D] (14) The word of the word 'includes" in the entry must, without unnecessary more, also include a caste which is a group of people. [393 E] (15) The word also includes a caste which may be a caste group, but does not include the caste group of individuals, but does include a caste of a group. The words 'including a caste group ' in the item refer to a tribe group of individuals are not to be construed as including a caste group which is a class independent of the Sunras caste. [391 F] (16) The word refers to a caste which includes a caste or group of persons but does not exclude a caste group from the Sunras Caste. [391 G] (17) The word used in the entry refers to a tribe or group of individuals and does not include caste group. It is only to be used in wider and wider sense.

The appellant was a tenant of a flat in the United Kingdom. He was in search of a partner to carry on his business during his intended absence. The police party, who were down below ready for the raid, held up the car of the appellant and recovered the sum of Rs. 29,500 and he was further charged under section 19(2) of the Act for receiving the said sum as a condition for the relin quishment of his tenancy. The police, who were over below ready for raid, held the car of appellant and recovered it. The police were recovered the bunch of keys and the documents that were handed over to the appellant by the appellant. The police also recovered the bunch and the documents which were handed over by the appellant to the appellant. On the appellant 's return to India, the police party recovered the bunch containing keys and the motor garage were handed over back to the appellant and the complainant. The police found the bunch of key and the documents handed over to him by the appellant and he was also charged under section 20(2) Of the Act for getting the same handed over to it. The appellant was charged under section 18(1) of the . The Magistrate convicted him under section 19 (2) of Act and sentenced him to one day 's simple imprisonment and a fine of Rs. 2,000 was also paid. The appellant appealed to the High Court. The High Court dismissed the appeal. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the offence arose only on receipt of any sum or any consideration as a condition of the relin tation by a tenant of his tenancy and that in the absence of a contract or local usage to the contrary, he entered into negotiations with the complain ant. HELD: (1) The consent of the landlord to an assignment is not necessary in the absence Of a contract or a local usage to that contrary.
