The appellant, who maintained a wage scale of Rs. 150/ and Rs. 150/- in the category of Draftsmen and Rs. 100/ in the case of other categories, was directed to pay the difference between the basic pay and dearness allowance and dearness allowance. The appellant challenged the award on the ground that the existing wage scales were fair and reasonable on a region cum industry basis and that it would not be possible for the appellant to bear the additional financial burden if the demands of the Union were accepted. The Industrial Tribunal rejected the contention of the appellant and held that the existing wages scales were fair, in paragraph 23 of the award, to give a flat increase of Rs. 100 in the category Of Draftsmen and that it was not possible for the workmen to bear the increased additional financial burden. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the award on two grounds: (1) that the existing pay scales were fair; (2) that the increase in the case was the one incorporated in the revised pay scales pertaining to different categories; (3) that the increased was the one which incorporated in the revision order, and (4) that the change was the one made in the revised wage scales pertaining to various categories. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the Tribunal had not given any ad hoc increase in the basic pay of individual workmen. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1)(a) The Tribunal was betrayed by a curious confusion in accepting the plea of the Union that a flat increase to the pay of each individual workman was intended in the original wage and, therefore, fell into the error of amending the award. [176C] (b) The Tribunal had only revised the wage scales by increasing the salary on entry into the service and never granted any ad hoc increases of salary to all employees. The omission of the words to each employee first after the figure Rs. 150 and again after the figure of Rs. 200/ and again after figure of Rs 200/ and Rs 200/ was added to the pay, of every other workman, who belonged to the Union staff, the financial load would increase to Rs. 150 / in the case where the category of Draughtsmen and Rs 100/ in that case of other category to the initial pay in the wage scales pertaining lo those categories. [176D] (c) The Tribunal, in making the award dated December 20, 1978, had clearly stated that all the employees were to get additional pay of Rs.150/ and Rs, 100/ respectively and might contend that the Tribunal, had only revised that the wage scales had necessarily to commence with figures Rs. 150. [176F] (d) The omission of a word to each employee immediately after the figure figure Rs. 100 and again after a figure of Rs 150/ and again thereafter after the figure was Rs. 200 / and Rs 200 / above the existing wage scale had necessarily to start with figures Rs 150/ above the existing pay scale. Immediately after the award was pronounced, while the iron was still hot as it were, the employees apparently realised that the employer might take advantage of the circumstance that it was never clearly mentioned in the award that all the employee were to getadditional pay of Rs 150 / and Rs. 200/- and Rs.100/ respectively and would contend that the tribunal had only revised it by increasing the pay on entry into service and never granting any ad hoc enhancement of salary to any employees. [176G H] (e) The Tribunal has clearly misdirected itself in accepting the contention of Union that a Flat increase to the Pay of each individual workmen was intended in a new wage structure and, therefore fell within the jurisdiction of the Tribunal.

The appellant was employed as a driver in a workshop of the respondent. The appellant was paid wages at the rate of Rs. 2,000 per month. The respondents contended before the authority that section 15 of the Act was inapplicable because the rates of wages fixed by the award did not fall within the definition of wages before the said definition was amended. The authority rejected the appellant 's contention that section 15 was applicable because the rates fixed by the said award did not come within the definition prescribed by section 2(vi) and it also argued that the claim of the respondents was barred by limitation. The appellant appealed to the authority under the Act. The authority did not decide the said question as a preliminary question because it held, and in our opinion, rightly, that section 15 did amount to wages as defined by section 2 (vi) and the claim of respondents was barred under section 15 of Act. Held, that the terms prescribed by an award, in law, constitute a fresh contract between the parties, and since an award made by an Industrial Tribunal cannot be said to amount to a contract of employment, the wage structure prescribed by the award cannot fall within the purview of section 2(vii). The terms prescribed by the said Act constitute a fresh agreement between the parties. The terms prescribed in an award, are not express and can be implied. But they must be terms which arise out of the contract of employment and since an Award made by an industrial Tribunal cannot be held to amount to contract of employment. The terms of the contract, in question need not be express and can, be implied. The terms in question need to be express and cannot be implied. It must be shown that they are terms which arise from the contract of appointment, and since the award made by the Industrial Tribunal cannot fall within section 2(viii), it is difficult to accede to the argument that the wages prescribed by the Award could not be treated as wages under section 2(iv) of the Act before it was amended. R. Chacko vs The State of Bombay, [1962] Supp. 1 S.C.R. 869, referred to.

The appellant was a Sub Divisional Officer in the Public Works Department, Pepsu. He was prosecuted under section 409 of the Indian Penal Code for having committed certain works at a place called Karhali. The trial Magistrate convicted him under section 465 and section 409 of Indian Penal Code. The High Court held that the evidence on record was insufficient to establish an offence either under section 465 or section 409 of that Code. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the prosecution was initiated without sanction under section 197(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure for his prosecution, that the evidence was insufficient to prove an offence either of under section 465 of the Indian penal Code and that there having been an acquittal of the appellant by the trial Magistrate, the materials on record did not justify a reversal of that verdict by the appellate Court. HELD: (1) The prosecution which has resulted in the conviction of the appellant was initiated without any sanction under section197(1) and therefore, sanction was required under section 197 of the Code. [1305 C] (2) The prosecution was initiated after the appellant was convicted and the absence of such sanc tion was fatal to the maintainability of the prosecution. [1306 D] (3) The prosecution did not prove the charge against the appellant. The prosecution did prove the charge. The prosecution was launched without any sanction. [1307 E] (4) The prosecution had resulted in the acquittal of the accused by the trial court. [1308 F] (5) The prosecution, therefore, did not prove that the thumb impression in the acquittance roll was that of the appellant. [1309 C] (6) The prosecution case was that the thumb impressions in the acquittsance roll were that of the accused. The appellant did not claim to have paid the amount to Parma, and the acquittances roll records the payment, and there was in acknowledgment thereof a thumb impression as against his name. [1310 F] (7) The prosecution proved that the thumb mark in the acquit tance roll was not that of the respondent. The appellant was prosecuted under sections 409 and 409 of the Penal Code. [1210 E] (8) The prosecution failed to prove the charge beyond reasonable doubt. [1311 F] (9) The prosecution could not prove the charges beyond reasonable doubt, and the absence thereof was fatal to it. [1312 F] (10) The prosecution has failed to prove that the appellant had paid the amount in question. The appellant had not proved that the signature in the acquitters roll was that or that he had affixed his thumb impression. [1313 G] (11) The prosecution also failed to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt and the absence was fatal to its maintainability. [1314 G] (12) The prosecution evidence was insufficient and the absence by such sanc ition was fatal to maintainability of the prosecutions. [1315 F] (13) The prosecution having resulted in the death of the appellant, the materials placed on record did no warrant a reversal of the verdict by the trial Court.

The assessee was a resident of Travancore State in the erstwhile State of Travancore. In 1941 income, profits and gains arose in British India and in the case of Travancore State income, profits or gains which a resident made in British India or in the case where the assessee sustains a loss of profits or gains in any year under any of the heads mentioned in section 9(1) (a) and (b) of the Travancore Act were exempted from tax. The Income tax Officer included the loss in the taxable income of the assessee. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the business losses incurred in the erstwhile Travancore State could be set off against the business profits made in the erstwhile States. The Appellate Tribunal held that the assessee was entitled to set off the loss against the business profit made in the former State of Travancore, and that the loss was not set off against profits made in British Indian States. The Tribunal held that business losses incurred by the assessee in the erstwhile Cochin State could be deducted from the profits made in Travancore State. The High Court in reference held that the loss incurred in the former Travancore State could not be set off under the head business profits made by the assessee. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the assessee that the first proviso to section 24(1) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, was not only affected the generality of the main enactment but also introduced an addendum that where the profits of the business arose in what was British India in the case, of the Travancore State income profits or gains under any other head, the losses could not by virtue of the proviso be deducted from profits made in India or Travancore State as the case may be. Held, that the mere use of the words loss of profits and gains to be, set off against profit and gains would not be sufficient to restrict the scope of the proviso to the profits and losses arising under the head Business in the two territories, i. e., British India and the Indian States. (1) that the intention of the Legislature was to restrict the set off of profits and losses in the two areas only to business or to modify the mode of computation under section 10 of the Indian Act. The mere use of words loss of profit or gains to be set off in business or to alter the mode of calculation under section 10 would not be enough to restrict the ambit of the proviso.

The respondent company was a public limited company. The company was a private limited company. It was a private company. The Company was a private Company. The company had been to retire its employees at the age of 55. The company resisted the workmen 's claim but submitted that it was agreeable to introduce for its Bombay employees provisions similar to those which had been introduced by agreement for the Calcutta employees retirement at the age Of 58 subject to the employees passing a medical examination on reaching the age of 58 subject to their employees passing a Medical examination on reaching that age of 55 subject to the employee passing a medical Examination on reaching the Age of 55. In the course of the hearing the workmen raised the age of retirement at 60 years. The Tribunal rejected the claim of the workmen on the ground that the trend in Bombay region had been to fix the retirement age at 60 years, that is, between 1952 and 1961, and that the trend had been to fixing the retirement age of clerical and subordinate staff at 60 years; that the Tribunal had found that in all the awards in recent times in various concerns in Bombay region the trend had not been to fix retirement age at 58 subject to employees passing a special medical examination on reaches the age of 60; that the trend of Bombay region to fix the age of superannuation at 60 years was not very commendable, and that its present conclusion that what was said by itself on an earlier occasion and was confirmed by this Court in appeal, was in fact inaccurate. The Tribunal held that in all these awards in recent time in Bombay region there was a general agreement that the age of retire should be fixed at 60. On a consideration of all the facts and circumstances disclosed by the oral and documentary evidence on this record, the Tribunal held that the trend was to fix the retire age at 60. The Tribunal also held that in the Bombay region at least there was a special agreement in the Bombay Region to fix the superannuation age of clerical staff at 60. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: The Tribunal had failed to notice that instances which may justify a revision of the judicial opinion expressed on an earlier occasions about a particular trend must be strong and unambiguous and they must speak for the period both before and more particularly after the previous finding had been recorded in the matter. [445C D] The Tribunal had not to notice any of the important material considerations in this connection. The Tribunal had found in all the Awards that in all those awards in recent years the trend had was to fix retirement ages at 60 years and that its previous finding that what was stated by itself on a earlier occasion and which was confirmed by the Court in appeal was in fact incorrect.

The appellants were tried and convicted for the same offence and received a like sentence. The High Court and the Court below drew from this the conclusion that the appellants were themselves the dacoits and convicted them accordingly under section 395 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced them to ' 5 years ' rigorous imprisonment and fine of Rs. 1,000/. The High court drew from this conclusion the conclusion that there was no other evidence in the case which points to the complicity of the appellants in the crime of dacoity and therefore as they could be suspected to be dacoits themselves, the only presumption to be drawn was one under section 41 1 722 of the Indian Evidence Act or at the most under section 412 of the Indian Indian Penal Code but not of complicity in the crime. The appellants appealed to this Court. HELD : (i) The presumption is stronger when the discovery of the fruits of crime is made immediately after the crime is. committed. When the discovery of fruits of crime was made immediately after a crime is. commit. and Disposal of the fruits thereof requires the finding of a person ready to receive them and the shortness of time, the nature of the property which is disposed of, that is to say, its quantity and its character determine whether the person who had the goods in his possession received them from another or was himself the thief or the dacoit. In some cases there may be other elements which may point to the way as to how the presumption may be drawn. They need not be stated here for they differ from case to case. [723 E F] (ii) The presumption must be stronger when the accused cannot be connected with the crime itself except by reason of possession of the fruits. [724 A B] (iii) The presumption under section 41 I 722 of the Evidence Act or under section 412 I.P.C. is stronger when there is some other evidence to show the complicity of an accused with the crime himself. [725 B] (iv) The presumption in this case that the persons with whom the goods were found were the dacoits themselves is a piece of evidence which connects him further with the crime.

The assessee firm applied to the Tribunal under section 66(1) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, to refer the following question to the High Court of Madras "Whether on the facts and in the circumstances of the case, the Tribunal was right in law in holding that the debt of Rs. 2,68,385/ written off as irrecoverable in the books of account was not one incurred in the course of money lending business of the assessee ?" The Tribunal rejected the application, but the Tribunal held that the debt was not one "accommodation" account to enable the Bombay firm to tide over the "financial crisis" threatening it in Samvat Year 2007, and that the trans actions in the account were totally unconnected with the normal business of the appellant. The High Court, however, held that the debts were due in respect of the business of the appellants other than money lending, and that, the trans actions of the assessee were totally unconnected With the normal business, profession or vocation, where accounts were not kept on the cash basis, if the debt was in respect of a loan made in the course Of the taxpayer 's business as a banker or money lender or when the taxpayer was carrying on any other business the debt was In respect of the other business of the respondent assessee, the High Court held that the amount of Rs. 1,68,386/ was not one 'accommodation ' account to enable Bombay firm to spread over the " financial crisis" threatening the Bombay firm, and that it was an "accommodation " account to enable a Bombay firm to reach tide over the financial crisis". The High Court also held that the Tribunal was wrong in holding that it was not right in law to allow the debt of the assessee in their books of account as irrecoverable debt representing loss sustained in the other business. The High court also held that in the circumstances, the Tribunal had rightly rejected the application. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) The debt of Rs 2,68,.385/ writtenoff as irrecoverable in its books of account, as irrecoverable in respect of business of the assesse was properly allowable in computing the taxable profits from business, profession, or vocation, and where accounts were kept on the Cash basis, if, the debt was a debt representing loss incurred in the other ' business, the debt is in respect of that other business. [12D E] (2) The Tribunal has found that the monies sent by the assessee to the Bombay firm were not loans made in the ordinary course of the money lending business, nor in respect of any other business of assessee. [12E] (3) The Tribunal had found that the moneys sent by the appellant to the Bombay Firm were not loans advanced in the ordinary sense of the business. [13E] (4) The Tribunal was right, in law in allowing the application, and in favour of the Department. [14E] (5) The Tribunal, in the present case, has found that there were three important circumstances which appear from the order of the Appellate Assistant Commissioner and the Income tax Officer from which it may be inferred that the advances made by the appellant were not loans. The Tribunal has also found that the amounts sent by the respondent to the Bombayfirm were not loans given in the ordinary way of the moneylending business of the assesses.

The appellant bank was a nationalised bank. The appellant bank was governed by the National Industrial Tribunal (Bank Disputes) Award of June 1962. The appellant Bank was governed by a scheme framed by the Central Government under section 7 of the Act. The scheme provided that the workmen would be fitted in the new scales of pay from January 1, 1962 on stage to stage adjustment basis, i.e., workmen who were drawing basic pay at a particular stage in the time scale of the Sastry award as modified would draw basic pay at the same stage in the new scale applicable to them under the Desai award as modified. The appellant 's case was that the Desai award provided that the workman would be fitted into the scale of pay from 1st January, 1959 on stage to date adjustment basis, and that the provision in the Sastry award was separated by the Labour Appellate Tribunal Decision from cl. (ii) of the Desai award, the adjusted basic pay in the new grade was not to exceed what point to point adjustment would give an employee on January 1, 1959. Held, that the High Court was right in holding that the Desai Award was not a modified award. The scheme of the Sastry Award was that the basic pay had to be fixed as on January 1. 1959, and the two increments provided by cl. (a) and (c) of cl. (iv) of cl.(ii) of cl (ii) had to be taken as on January January 1,1959. The scheme was that the workmen should be fitted in new scales of wages from January 1. 1962 on stage basis, i,e., workmen drawing basic pay in a particular scale. The scheme did not provide for any revision of the scales of pay. The scheme had to be worked out as on January1, 1959, and it was not open to the appellant bank to contend that the provision of the Sastry Tribunal Award was separated by cl. 5. The scheme, therefore, did not provide that the workmen could be fitted in a new scale of pay as modified by placing him at the stage in the Sastry Award scale equal to or next above his basic pay as on January. 1, 1959, in the scale then in force in the bank concerned.

The workmen of the Company were granted sick leave for 7 days sick leave on full pay and dearness allowance in 1958 subject to the condition that the benefit would cease to apply when the benefits of the Employees ' State Insurance Scheme would become available to the workmen. The workmen of the company were granted sick Leave for 7 days in the case of a, spell of sickness following, at an interval of not more than 15 days, the spell of sickness for which sickness benefit was last paid. The workmen also claimed that they were entitled to the sickness benefit for the first two days of sickness except in the case where a spell of sickness was last paid, and also that the reasonableness of the demand could not be examined by the Tribunal. The Tribunal rejected the claim of the workmen on the ground that the sickness benefit was not adequate for the first three days of sickness. The workmen appealed to the High Court. The High Court dismissed the appeal. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the workmen that the Tribunal had wrongly interpreted the word "accident" in section 49 of the Act and that the Tribunal should not have given the benefit of 7 days sick Leave, and that the workmen did not deserve anything more than sickness benefit for their first two days also. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The Tribunal has cor rectly examined the controversy and given adequate reasons for allowing the benefit of the sick leave with retro spective effect from January 1, 1975 in the case. Such a leave could not be categorised as privilege leave as, by its very nature, it would be admissible only in the case, of actual sickness certified by a registered medical practitioner. It appears, however, that it was not necessary, in the circumstances of the case, to award the benefit of sick leave with retrospective effect from January l, 1975 in view of the fact that the Tribunal has correctly examined, the controversy and gave adequate reasons for awarding the benefit of 8 days sick leave in the manner set out in the award. Such a Leave could not be regarded as privilege leave. [864 D E] 2. The Tribunal had cor rectently examined the controversy, and given adequate reason for allowing the benefits of 7 days Sick leave in the way set out in its award. Such leave could not, therefore, be categorised as leave as, By its very nature it would be inadmissible only in the cases of actual sickness Certified by a registered Medical practitioner. It would be admissible even in the case in actual sickness certified as a registered medical Practitioner. It would, therefore, not be correct to say that what has been awarded by the Tribunal is additional privilege leave as. by its very character, it would not be admissible for the first four days of sickness, except in the cases where actual sickness certified is certified by a Registered medical practitioner. [865 F G] 3. The Tribunal was not justified in giving the benefit of 6 days sick leave with absolutely spective effect on the ground of sickness benefit. [866 F] 4. The Tribunal, therefore, was not justified by giving the benefit to the sick leave. [876 F] 5. The Tribunal should not, in any view of the matter, have given the benefits of sick leave, and that it works out to about half the average average wage of a workman, and even that amount is not admissible for the second two days of sick leave except in the ease of actual sickness.

The grounds were not vague and no details of the activities allegedly carried on by him were given. The High Court dismissed the petition. Held, that the grounds furnished in this case were open to the challenge of vagueness, the further question which arises is whether the validity of the order of detention can be sustained by reason of the claim, in public interest, of non disclosure of facts made by the Under Secretary to the Government of Bombay by means of his affidavit filed in the High Court. The right of the detenue to be furnished particulars, is subject to the limitation under article 22(6) of the Constitution. The right to be furnished the particulars is subject to limitation under article 23(6) which provides that disclosure of facts considered to be against public interest cannot be required. The right is subject to limitations under article 22 (6) which expressly excludes the right of representation. The right conferred by article 22(5) to the extent of denying all particulars and leaving the grounds absolutely vague. The right under article 22 is subject to restrictions under article 22. The right extends not only to the right of the detenu to be furnished, but also to the right to be afforded a proper opportunity of representation. Such a right is subject subject to the limitations under article 23 (6) of which disclosure of facts is subject to a limitation under article 19(6) whereby disclosure of facts consider to be against the public interest cannot not be implied in these circumstances. If the appellant bad exercised his right to ask for particulars, at the time, from the detaining authority, there can be no doubt that he would have been furnished then the very information which has been supplied in paragraph 12 of the Under Secretary 's affidavit in answer to para 15(g) of the appellant 's petition, both of which have been already set out above.

The appellants contended that the conciliation proceedings had continued for a period of more than 14 days as from January 17, 1952, and that the conciliation proceeding had continued for more than 14 months as from January 18, 1952, when the appellant No. I was asked to appear before the Conciliation Officer on January 9, 1952, the appellant No, I was asked by the Conciliation Officer to appear before him on January 9. 1952, and after getting one adjournment the appellant No., I was asked again to appear before a Conciliation Officer on February 9, 1952. The appellant contended that the Conciliation Officer had no jurisdiction to make the report and that the proceedings had continued beyond the period of 14 days as provided in section 20(2)(a) of the . Held, that the conciliation Proceedings were pending at the time when the appellant was dismissed. The conciliation proceedings were pending at that time when the order of dismissal was passed. The conciliation proceeding were pending at a time when the report under section 12(6) was made by the Conciliation officer but when that report was received by the appropriate Government. The conciliation Proceedings were not pending at the date when the report was received. The conciliation was pending at the stage when the report of the Conciliation Officer was received by it. The conciliation could be continued even after the report was sent to the appropriate Government, and the proceedings closed within a fortnight and if proceedings were not closed, as they were in the present case, or if the Conciliation Officer did not make his report within 14 days he may be guilty of a breach of duty but in law the proceedings do not automatically come to an end after 14 days but only terminate as provided in s 20(2) (b) of that Act. The conciliation process was pending at that stage when the appellant had been dismissed. The proceedings were pending when the appellant 's report was received and the proceedings were closed. The conciliation had to be held to terminate when the report is received by the Government. The proceedings therefore did not end when the report received by the competent Government. The provisions of the Act were not applicable to the proceedings under the Act.

The appellant firm was granted a licence for exhibition of cinematographs in the cinema theatre known as Apsara Theatre. The licence was renewed by the District Magistrate in the name of Ved Gupta. On April 27, 1979, a suit was instituted against Ved Gupta and seven others by seven of the partners including Krishan Kumar for a declaration that the Cinema licence dated July 22, 1969 issued by the District Collector, Jammu was the property of the firm Apsara Cinema and for a prohibitory injunction restraining defendants 1 to 7, namely, Shri Ved Gupta and six of the partners who were residing with him from interfering with the running of the Cinema by the plaintiffs and also for a prohibitory order restraining defendants 1 and 7 from interfering with running of the cinema by the plaintiffs. The District Magistrate rejected the said request by a detailed order dated April 21, 1979. The District Collector held that the renewal of the licence could not be made in the name o the partnership firm Apsra Theatre and that the cinema licence dated July 23, 1969 issued in the name Of Ved Gupta was the property in respect of the Apsara theatre. The District Judge also held that the licence in respect of Apsara cinema was the property and the licence could be suspended. The State Government preferred an appeal to the High Court. The High Court dismissed the appeal. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the District Magistrate had no power under the Act or the Rules to make such an order. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The District magistrate had no power to suspend the licence. [578C] 2. The District Magistrates had no power Under the Act or Rules to make an order. The only other reason stated by the High Court for quashing the District Magistrate 's order is that the District magistrate had jurisdiction to suspend the cinema licence. [579D] 3. The only reason stated by this Court for quashing of the District Magistrate's order is that under the provisions of the Act the power to suspend a licence is conferred only by Section 6 F of the Act as one implicit in the larger power of revocation and unless the conditions precedent mentioned in the said Section are present, the licensing authority had no jurisdiction to suspend it. [579C] 4. The only another reason stated by it for quashing the order passed by the District magistrate directing the suspension of cinema shows in the Theatre cannot be said to have visited the writ petitioners with any adverse civil consequences. [579F] 5. The only one reason stated by High Court for quashed the District Magistrate "that under the provisions o the Act the powers to suspend a licensee are conferred only by section 6 F of . The only other reasons stated by the District Magistrates for quashing the impugned order is that "the District Magistrate had jurisdiction to suspended the cinema licence".

The appellants, who were the owners of the mills and the factory in question, were granted leases of the mills for a period of five years on the terms and conditions set out therein. On 12 2 1954 the appellants appeared before the respondent, and contended that he had no auth ority to issue the notice in question under section 12, and that it was therefore illegal. The respondent contended that the notice, Exhibit C, was ultra vires the powers of the Custodian under that section. Held, that the rights of the appellants in so far as they related to the purchase by them of the mills, and the factory were not affected by the sale in favour of the appellants, were not affected. The notice in terms refers to the lease which it is proposed to cancel, and secondly to the movables in respect of which directions were given. In the present case, the notice, Ex. C, was to that extent without juris,diction, and that the respondent should accordingly be prohibited from cancelling that portion of the document. The notice, Ex C, was not to that extent as it was originally intended to cancel the lease. The notice was to that effect. The notice did not specify the period of limitation. The notice merely stated that the notice was to the effect that the notice should be cancelled. The notice only stated that the appellants had systematically committed breaches of the various terms on which the properties bad been leased to them. The notice also stated that the movables were leased to the appellants for a period for five years on payment of the price fixed by the Custodian. The notice stated that the appellant had systemaously committed breaches of various terms on the terms set out therein, and that he had always the power to cancel leases created not merely by the evacuees but also by himself. The notice further stated that the respondent had systemaly committed breaches of certain terms on which he had been leased to the appellant. The notice therefore did not specify any period of limitation, and the notice did not mention any period of time. The notice could not be said to be invalid merely because the notice did mention the period of time for the cancellation of the lease.

The appellant, a newspaper employee, was employed in the Indian Post Offices, Calcutta. He was working as a newspaper employee in the Indian Posts Offices. The appellant was appointed as an employee of the Indian Postal Services. He was promoted as an employee in the Calcutta Postal Service. The appellant challenged the order of his transfer before the Central Administrative Tribunal. The Tribunal accepted the plea of the appellant and declared that the law reports were not newspapers within the meaning of section 2(b) of the Act and that the demand made by the Deputy Labour Commissioner to comply with the order made by the Central Government on the basis of the recommendations of Justice Palekar were unsustainable by its judgment dated 22nd April, 1983. The High Court accepted the plea and declared that a law journal Cuttack Law Times, which was a non official monthly journal containing the decisions of the Orissa High Court, the Orissa Board of Revenue and also of the Supreme Court of India and of the High Courts in India which are supplied to it by its agents appointed at New Delhi and other places where High Courts are situated. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The law reports published by the Ist respondent are newspapers and the employees employed by the Ist Respondent in their production or publication of the said law reports should be extended the benefit of the orders passed by the Central Administrative Tribunals on the basis on the recommendations made by the Palekar Award. [782G H] 1.2 The law reports of the Ist respondent contain information about the recent events which have taken place in the Supreme Court or in the High Courts which are public bodies and these are matters in which the public is interested. [785A] 1.3 The law reports publish by the Ist appellant are newspapers and are the matters in which public is interested, [785B] 1.4 The expression `newspaper ' as defined in the Act includes not merely `public news ' but also `comments on public news and information. The Act in question is a beneficent legislation which is enacted for the purpose of improving the conditions of service of the employees of the newspaper establishments and hence even if it was possible to have three opinions on the interpretation of the provisions, the one whose views are being published by the Central Legislature has to be accept. [786C] 1.5 The law reports are published by the 1st respondent are newspapers, and the employees engaged by the Ist respondents in their production and publication of the aforesaid law reports should, be extended the benefits of the orders made by the State Government on the ground that they contain information about recent events which took place in the High Court or in any High Courts which were public bodies and those are matters in Which the public are interested. [787D] 1.6 The expression `public news or comments on public news ' as defined under the Act includes also `comment on public news or comments '. [790B] 1:7 The expression `oldspaper ' is defined by section 2(c) of the , as any working journalist, and includes any other person employed to do any work in, or in relation to, any newspaper establishment. It is significant that the expression `new ' as defined by the Act includes `public news and information '.

[231B] 1.2 The respondent was in occupation on 1st January, 1973 under an subsisting agreement for a licence. good deal of submission was made before the High Court and it was directed that the appellant should be heard afresh in accordance with law because in a previous decision Vaidya, J. by the judgment dated 9th December, 1975 as mentioned hereinbefore had allowed the appellant 's appeal. [231F] 1.5 The respondent was, therefore, a licensee and was not a licensee. [231G] 1.6 The respondent was entitled to continue in occupation till a decree for eviction was passed. [231H] 1.7 The respondent was the licensee and not the sub tenant. [232B] 1:8 The respondent was admittedly in occupation of premises under a valid subsisting agreement for the licence. good dealt of submission was also made before the Small Cause Judge. The appellants were the sellers of the agricultural produce in the State of Madras. The appellants were the purchasers of the agricultural land in the State. The appellants claimed that they were not prohibited from holding the market as property, for they could still utilise it for commodities other than the notified crops. The State Government rejected the appellants ' claim and the High Court held that the appellants had really two fundamental rights: one was to carry on trade or business and the other was to hold their property, i.e., the market; that by reason of the notification they were not prevented from doing their business, for they can still do business in the market established subject to the regulations and also do business outside the prescribed area; and that the appellants were not prohibited by the Act. Held, that the appellants have really two fundamental right: one is to carry on business or business and that the other is to hold their properties, i. e., the market and the other is also to hold their business, i.ee., the market. The appellants had no right to carry on their trade or business. The appellants have no right to do business in their trade or their business. The question whether the allowance described as I mahimai is a trade allowance depends upon the nature of that deduction. If the payment is de hors the terms of the transaction but made towards consideration for the use of the premises or services rendered, it would not be a deduction from the price or commodity within the meaning of section 14 of the Act.

The petitioner was appointed as officiating Executive Engineer in Class I service under the Ministry of Works and Housing in Government of India and was compulsorily retired by order dated 3.8.1976 with effect from 5.11.1976. He was reverted to the post of Assistant Engineer in officiating position and was con tinuing in that post when he was compulsorily retired. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The petitioner was not a Government servant in Class I Service or post. [655G] 1.2 The purpose of Fundamental Rules 56(j) is to confer power on the appropriate authority to compulsorily retire Government servant in the public interest and the classification of Government servants into two categories and sub clause (i) takes within its sweep those Government servants who at the relevant time were in Class I, or Class II Service or post, whether substantively, temporarily or on officiating basis. [657D] 1.4 The object of the sub clause is to confer Power on the appropriate Government to compulsorily retire Govt servant in the Public interest and the classify of Government servants in two categories and Sub clause (i), takes within its ambit those Government servants which at the relevant date are in Class I services or post, either substantively, temporarily, or on officiating or ad hoc basis. [613E F] 1.5 The purpose of sub clauses (i) and (ii) has a purpose underlying it. If a Government servant belonging to a class I or ClassII service or post is in Class I Class II serviceor post, he has no rights to the post or can always be promoted to the post, if no, on which, he has a lia tion. [658G] 1:6 The purpose of Rule 56(J) is to conferring power on the competent authority to compulsorily retiring Government servant in class I or class II service or posts on substantive, temporary or offi ciating basis. If the Servi tion is not bring to an end either reverting the Government Servant to his substantive office before the power is exercised,the Government servant con sidered must be taken in to be in class I and Class I or classII service or posts at the relevant place and would come within the ambit of sub clause (1). The appellant was appointed as a clerk by the Panchayat Samiti in 1963 long before the Amending Act came into force on June 13, 1973. He was, therefore, entitled to be absorbed in Government service as a clerk in any event. But, as a result of the deletion of section 33 of the Act by the Amending Act of 1973, the appellant was entitled to be considered for promotion to the post of a Head Clerk. The appellant was appointed on June 1, 1963 by the Panchayat Samitis in 1963 long after the Amending Act. On March 14, 1975, the appellant, was appointed as Head Clerk on June 1. 1973 by the Panchayat Parishad. On March 13, 1975, he was promoted as a Head Clerk on an ad hoc basis. On March 15, 1975, a resolution was passed by the Panchayat Adhikari, Loharu, which was published in the Haryana Gazette on June 13. 1973, whereby the appellant was appointed to the post. The appellant, however, was appointed on April 1, 1975 by the Panchayat Parishads in 1963 long prior to the Amending Act, 1973. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court of Punjab and Haryana, asking that he should be absorbed as a Head clerk. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the right to be considered was a term and condition of service, and that the appellant was not entitled to be treated for promotion. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the right of the appellant to be considered in the post of Head Clerk prior to his absorption in Government service had to be recognised and protected, despite the fact that such appointment was made after June 13,1973 when the Amending Act was brought into force. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The right to be treated as a term and conditions of service, what is relevant for our purpose is not whether the appellant was entitle to be considered to be promoted but whether the Panchayat Samiti had the right to appoint him to the post on which it purported to do so. Clearly, it had fortified that right on June 13 1973. It could not, therefore, have appointed the appellant as a Head Office, as it purported to doing, in January 1974 on an adhoc basis. [775C D] 1.2 The appointment of the appellant as Head Clerk being without the authority of law, the Government was not bound to absorb him in the post. [776F] 1.3 The appointment of appellant to the post was made after July 13, 1973 when the Amending Acts came into force. [778G] 1.4 The appointment of a Head clerk being without the sanction of law, it could not have been appointed validly. [782C] 1.5 The appointment of an appellant to the posts of Head Clerk being not without the authority, of law, he was appointed lawfully to the post and that is the post in which the Government has absorbed him. [768D] 1.6 The appointment of respondent to the post is not without the sanction or authority of law. [767E] 1.7 The appointment of Shri S.R. Gupta, as Head Clerk was without the authority or law, the government was not bound by absorb him in Government service. He was appointed lawfully by the Panchayat fy on an ad ad hoc basis in January 1974 or the further fact that he was appointed as the Head Clerk on April 1. 1975, on a regular basis. The appointment of his appellant to the said post being without the approval of law, his appointment as a Head Cashier was not valid. [766E] 1:6 The appointment to the post by the Panchayat being without the consent of the Governor, the Government had the right under section 14(4) of the Amending Act to make appointments to the Panchayat.

The appellants were displaced persons from West Pakistan. They were allotted quasi permanent allotment of 24 standard acres and 15 3/4 units in the village of Raikot in Ludhiana District in 1949. The Custodian General recommended to the Custodian General the restoration of the land to the 14 allottees who had been taken away from them by reason of cancellation of the allotment in their favour by the order dated October 31, 1952. The appellants ' application was rejected by the Deputy Custodian General on the ground that his jurisdiction to revise the order had been taken over by virtue of the provisions of , (44 of 1954) and the notification issued thereunder on March 24, 1955. The appellants then filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the order on the ground, inter alia, that the order had not been passed by the Custodian General and that the notification issued under section 12(1) of the with respect to any property or class of property would be in conflict with section 10 of the Act. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the order of the Custodian General was not a nullity because the notification issued by the Central Government under section 12 of the with regard to any property was published in the official Gazette of that State dated March 24,1955, and that the Notification issued thereunder on the 23rd July, 1949, had become functus officio with respect to it and could not be said that section 19(1) was completely in conflict with the section 10 of 1954 Act. Held, that the notification dated March 24. 1955, was not a valid notification because the notification was published in a official Gazette of the State dated March 25, 1955, and the notification was not a final notification. The notification was published on March 24.1955 and the notification had become functusly officio with respect of it and could no be said that it was a final notification under section 12.

The appellant, a mahant of the Dera, was appointed mahant of a Dera. He was elected to be the mahant of Dera. The respondent, who was the mahant, died on 13 10 1970. The appellant, who was a mahant, filed a suit for possession of the DMO and the properties attached to it. The suit was filed on the basis that the appellant as the lawfully appointed mahant was entitled to manage the properties of the Dhoh. The trial court decreed the suit. The High Court, on appeal, held that after the death of Som Dass, as his Chela "inherited the sum total of the rights which earlier vested in Som Dass and when a controversy was raised about such rights, then the appellant was bound to bring on record the legal representatives of the deceased within the time prescribed by law. Dismissing the appeal, the Court, HELD: 1. The suit is for possession and management of the Dioh. When a suit is brought by or against a person in a representative capacity and there is a devolution of the interest of the representative, the rule that has to be applied is Order 22, rule 10, and not rule 3 or 4, whether the devolution takes place as a consequence of death or for any other reason. [448C D] 2. The suit, therefore, was for possession and control of the Dieh. The suit could be continued by or against the person to or upon whom such interest has come or devolved. [449E] 3. The suit being for possession and ownership of the D eera and the properties appertaining to it by the appellant purporting to be the de facto mahant against Som Dass, the rule of limitation for impleading them under Order 22, Rule 10 will apply. [447C] 4. The suit for possession and administration of the Dooh and the properties belonging to it by virtue of his election as mahant subsequent to the death of the mahant subsequent thereto, the rule is based on the principle that trial of a suit cannot be brought to an end merely because the interest of a party in the subject matter of the suit has devolved upon another during the pendency of the suit but that suit may be continued against the person acquiring the interest with the leave of the Court. [446C] 5. The suit in the instant case was for possession, and management of properties appertaining to the Dera and its properties and it devolved upon shiam Dass by virtue of the election as mahants of the Dia. The suit therefore was for possession. [445D] 6. The suit having been filed on the ground that the appellant was lawfully appointed mahants of Dera, the suit was for possession or management of the properties appertaining thereto. [440E] 7. The suit filed on the date of the death of Dieh was not for possession and the appellant was entitled to be in possession of the properties. [442E] 8. The suit had been filed on a basis that the respondent was lawfully appointed as mahant of that Dera. [443F] 9. The suit as filed on the strength of the title of the appellant, was for the possession and management and management of that Dioh and the property appertaining to it. [444F] 10. The suit fell within the ambit of Order 22, r. 10. The appellant was not entitled to prosecute the appeal. [439F] 11. The appeal was, therefore, dismissed.

The appellant was the owner of certain goods. The goods were exported by the appellant. The goods remained the sellers ' property till the goods had crossed the customs barrier and thus entered the export stream. The goods had been brought on board the ship and so the sales were exempted from tax under article 286(1)(b) of the Constitution. The appellant contended that the goods remained the seller ' property till they crossed the customs frontier and therefore the sales were exempt from tax under articles 286(1) (b) and (c) of the constitution. Held, that the words " a person " in section 10(b) of Bombay Sales Tax Act as a " registered dealer " and that the words used in the section are " a registered dealer to whom he sells the goods. The words " a registered " dealer " in section 8(b) are not intended to be used in the sense that the property is intended to pass and does pass on the shipment of the goods. In the present sales the property in the goods passed to the buyers on shipment. The goods did not pass to the buyers. The goods could not be said to have been despatched by him or by a person to whom he sold the goods. It was not necessary that the goods should be despatched by him to the buyers at the time of the export. The words ' a person " were used in the context of the export and the words " another person " were intended to be construed as used in the provision. The words used in section 8 of the Bombay Sales Tax (Amendment) Act, 1947, are not intended merely to be used for the purpose of the export but are intended to be in the nature of a contract. The words are used in the same sense as the words " other person" in section 8. The words were used in different senses and they are used in different contexts. The words in section 8 are intended to indicate that the property was intended to pass or do on the shipment. The words must be construed as meaning only those persons who are not a registered dealer as sufficient. The words cannot be used in a sense which is not intended to take in the context in which they are used. The words of the section are intended to convey the idea that the property should pass to the buyer at some point of time before shipment. The word " a person" in the section cannot be used to convey the intention of the Legislature to levy purchase tax on a person who has given such certificate under section 8(a). The words must, therefore, be construed as including those persons who were not a registered dealers as sufficient.

The appellant, a married woman, was married to the respondent on April 1, 1962. The appellant, a widow, was married in 1962. The respondent, a married daughter, was married on April 1. 1962. The husband, however, was not a party to the petition. The appellant filed a petition for maintenance under section 125 of the Criminal Procedure Code, 1973, for the maintenance of herself and her child. The Magistrate who tried the petition for maintenance held that the appellant was a subsisting wife and awarded monthly maintenance of Rs. 400/ for the mother for her subsistence, taking due note of the fact that the cost of living in Bombay where the parties lived, was high, and that the respondent had provided residential accommodation to the appellant. The Magistrate, who tried the case, held that the respondent was a subsisting husband and awarded monthly allowance of Rs. 300/ for the maintenance and the appellant was entitled to an allowance. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The language of section 125(4) (b) is manifestly to recognise the substitute maintenance arrangement by lump sum payment organised by the custom of the community or the personal law of the parties. There must be a rational relation between the sum so paid and its potential as provision for maintenance. The concept of maintenance is not confined to the amount so paid and the potential as provision of maintenance. [81C D] 1.2 The language of the Explanation (a) to section 127(3) (b), is manifestly to recognize the substitute maintenance arrangements by lump sum payments organised by the customs of the community, or the personal Law of the parties,. There must, therefore, a rational relation to the object and is thus clear how this innovative and sensitive provision with a benignant disposition towards destitute divorcees has been overlooked by all the courts below. [81D E] 1.3 The object of the payment 'under any customary or personal law ' must be to obviate destitution of the divorcee and to provide her with wherewithal to maintain herself. The whole scheme of section 127(4) is manifestly clear to recognise the substitution of maintenance arrangement by lumpsum payment organised by custom of the Community or the personal laws of the parties.[81E] 1.4 The whole scheme is manifestly to recognition the substitute maintenance Arrangement by lump sum paid organised by the Custom of the community and to provide Her with wherew aids to maintain herself, [81F] 1.5 The object of payment 'under no customary or personal Law ' must be To obviate destitution and to provide she with whereworts to maintain herself; the obligor, not pro tanto but wholly. The purpose of the payment is manifestly to obviate destitute of the divorceee and to provide She with wherew Assistance to maintain herself and to provide for her with whereWithal to maintain her. [81G] 1.6 The whole scheme, therefore, is manifestly to recognised the substitute maintenance agreement by lump sum pay organised by the rule of the community. [81F G] 1.7 The scheme of section 125 (4) (a) is manifestlyto recognise the substitute Maintenance arrangement by lump sums payment organised by a custom of the public or the personallaw of the parties; and the obligor not pro tantos. The object of paying maintenance is certified by the fulfilment of the social obligation, not by a ritual exercise rooted in custom.

The appellant, a tenant in respect of a building, leased out a portion of the building to the respondent. The respondent filed a suit for eviction on the ground that the building was let out to the appellant. The appellant contended that since the subject matter of the lease under exhibit P 1 was only a vacant site, the Rent Controller had no juris diction to fix the fair rent in respect thereof and that, therefore, the claim in the suit for arrears of rent based on the Rent Controller 's order in respect of the premises covered by exhibit P 1 had to fail. The Rent Controller rejected the contention of the appellant and held that the building on the land leased under exhibit P1 had also been conveyed to the LIC and that the LIC was entitled to seek fixation of fair rent in regard to the premises covered under exhibit P I. The respondent preferred an appeal to the High Court. The High Court dismissed the appeal. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that since the property was only a " vacant site", the Rent Controller has no juris dic tion to fix the rent in respect of that premises and that, consequently, the claim for arrears of Rent based on the rent fixation order in respect thereof had to fail, and that, in the instant case, the Rent controller had no jurisdic tion to determine the fair rent of item 1 at Rs.994 p.m. and that, accordingly, the claim was barred by section 12(4) of the Act. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The question on which the jurisdiction of the civil court is excluded is only the determination as to the fair rent payable by the tenant to the landlord because that is a matter squarely and exclusively within the jurisdiction of Rent Controller and, therefore, impliedly excluded from the purview of the civil Court. [549G] 1.2 The question on what the jurisdiction of civil court is ousted is only the determining as to the final rent of the premises. If, and only if, this relationship exists between the parties, the Rent Control Act, the question on which jurisdiction of the Civil Court is excluded is merely the determination as a matter of law. If, however, this relationship existed between the parties. the Rent Controller steps in for a limited purpose to determine what the fair rent is and then fades out of the picture. If, or only if, the relationship exists between them, the Rent Rent Controller steps In for a limited Purpose to determine what fair rent is, and then fade out of the story. In the instant case it was the latter and such decision on the nature or character of the land has been given a finality under section 64 C which cannot be ques tioned in a court of law. [549H; 549A] 1.3 The question on the basis of which the jurisdiction is excluded is not one of the direct issues before the Rent Controller. If, & only if, it is, that this relationship exists both between the parties the Rent Controller step in for a restricted purpose to determine the rent payable by t he tenant to the landlords. If, therefore, this relationship exist between the parties and the Rent Controller proceedings in this case had come to the conclusion that there is a relationship of landlord and a tenant and that the appellant LIC was entitled only to recover the rent from the tenants, it will have to pass a decree in favour of the LIC on the basis that the question may have had to be considered by the Rent tribunals as a collateral issue in deciding certain applications before them.

The petitioner was a respondent who had not appeared before the High Court, and, therefore, could not be heard by the High Court. The petitioner filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the final seniority list. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioner that the petitioner was not heard after the final list was prepared. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The petitioner respondent was entitled to an opportunity to object to the proposed assign ment of a place to him in the seniority list. [828G] 1.2 The petitioner respondent had been unable to make out, in their petitions, any grounds for interference with the final list. [829G] 1:3 The petitioner respondent 's case was that he was not heard before the final list is prepared. He was not heard at the final list, and, as the petitioner was unable to make a further representation against even a final seniority list, the opportunity afforded was to be given before the final lists were to be declared and published as a final list. The petitioner respondent could not possibly be heard by us. [828C] 1:4 The petitioner respondent, who is the respondent before us, was unrepresented, Mrs. (1) from which, learned Counsel thought, the following observations could perhaps be cited on behalf of him: "The petitioner respondent was claiming relief against the final seniority lists although he was given due opportunity to object, to the provi sional list. The question is whether the petitioner should have a further opportunity against even a provisional seniority list. If he was to have that opportunity the list would not really be final but only provisional or preliminary. Roy 's case (supra) was decided on entirely irrelevant and extraneous consideration. [828A] 1:5. The petitioner was not entitled to an additional opportunity to object against the final list on some such grounds of invalidity, those grounds had to be shown to exist. [828B] 1:6. The petitioner 's case is also covered by Shankariah 's case. [828F] 1:7. The petitioner had been unable, to make out a case for interference with final list. If the petitioner was to have a further chance against even a tentative seniority list, he could not possibly have a further right against even a preliminary seniority list. But, once he had that opportunity, it cannot possibly be said that he should have a more opportunity against even the final seniority. [828D] 1:8. The petitioner is not entitled to any additional opportunity to make a representation against the final gradation list. [825C] 1.9. The petitioner, therefore, cannot be heard by this Court. [828E] 1:10. The petitioner has been unable to show, in their petition, any grounds, for interference with their final list. It is not within the province of the Courts to lay down what are in the principles to be adopted for purposes of equation. If that is established, the decision of the authorities concerned will have to stand. If a particular decision is mala fide or arrived at on totally irrelevant and extraneous considerations, such a decision can be interfered with by Courts. [828H] 1:11. The petitioner could not possibly make out, that he should had a further opportunity to object. The respondents were entitled to an adequate opportunity to make representation with regard to the two points urged by the petitioner respondent before the final gradation lists were to he declared and published. [828AB] 1:12. The petitioner did not make out, as was the case of the petitioner in Prabhavalkar 's case, any grounds of invalidity. Those grounds have to be shown. [828 E] 1:13.

Dismissing the petitions, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The petitioners who are granted Additional licences on the basis that they have been granted Additional Licences prior to April 01, 1988, are to be treated at par with Export Houses who have been granted additional licences under the import and Export Policy 198891. [236E] 1.2 The petitioners who have been denied Additional licences under Import & Export Control Policy 1978 79 have to be treated as persons similarly circumstanced as Export House who are granted additional licences for a much lesser value under the Import Policy 1988 91 on the basis Of the net foreign exchange earnings. [236F] 1.3 The petitioners who who are granted the Additional licences under import and Export Control Policy 1988 91 have to be regarded at par with export Houses who are granted Addl licences under the Imports & Export Policy 1988 92 on the basis on the order Dated April 18,1985, under the Import& Export Policy 1978 91. The respondents were the manufacturers of excisable goods. They were selling the goods to the buyers. The respondents were the buyers of the goods. The respondents sold the goods to their buyers. The goods were delivered to the buyers in packed condition and the containers were not returnable by the buyer. The respondents filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the vires of the Act. The High Court held that the cost of packing was includible in the assessable value. The High court held that the value of packing materials including those supplied by the buyer, had to be included in the assessable valuation. In the appeals to this Court it was contended on behalf of the respondents that the cost incurred by the manufacturer in packing of the drums was includible in assessable value. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. The cost of packing envisaged in section 4(4)(d)(i) of the Act for determining the "value" in relation to any excisable goods is only the "cost of such pack ing" incurred by the manufacturers and recovered from the buyer except where the packing is of durable nature and is returnable by the buyers to the assessee. The "cost of packing" referred in section 4 (4)(d) does not in clude within its ambit the cost of the packing not incurred by the assessee when the packing is supplied by the assessee and not the manufacturer. [982D] 2. The cost for packing envisaged in Section 4(4) (d)(i), does not in elude within its purview the cost of such packaging not incurred by him when the packing was supplied by the manufacturer and recovered from his buyer except where, the packing is returnable by, the manufacturer levies a charge for the packing which is intrinsically and inevitably incidental to placing the manufactured goods on the market. [983E] 3. The cost incurred by manufacturer in packing is only the cost of a durable nature. The " cost of such packing" referred to in section 4 of the Act, for determining the value of such goods, is only the 'cost of such packing which is attributable to the manufacturer and recoverable from the buyer. [984F] 4. The " Cost of such packing", referred in section 3(4)(b)(i) does not mean the cost of any packing. [985F] 5. The cost is not the cost of "cost of any packing" incurred by a manufacturer when the packing becomes returnable. [986F] 6. The "packing" referred in Section 4 (4) (b)(i), is not in cluding within its ambit to the cost of pack ing not incurred by manufacturer when the pack is supplied by him and not the manufacturers. [987F] 7. The "market value" referred in sub clause (ii) does not include the cost of 'packing of goods '.
