The appellant was a private Devasthan or a public religious trust. The deity of his worship was Shri Vithal Rukhamai. The deity was the founder of the temple. The deity installed in the temple was intended by the Founder to be continually worshipped by an indeterminate multitude of the Hindu public. The deity also installed in the Temple a temple. The temple was managed by the saints in succession nominated by the reigning saint. The deity continued to be worshipped by the saint. In accordance with this theory, it was held by the Charity Commissioner that the property was a public religious endowment. The Sanad being an ancient Royal grant was a very important piece of evidence to show that though Sakharam Maharaj, the founder of a temple, had already been succeeded by Guru Govindbuwa and the latter by Balkrishnabuwa, the land had been held in the year 1860 61 in the name of the Devasthan. In the absence of anything to the contrary of a convincing nature, a grant by the Government in favour of the temple describing the property to be in charge of a manager leads to an inference that the property is a public religious endowments. The Sanads were made with the object of maintenance of the worship of the deity for the benefit of the Hindu community as a whole. The appellant contended that the Sansthan was a private property and it was also transferred to the Shishya Adhikari to maintain it as his own property. Held, that the Sansthan and the temple are public religious endowments within the meaning of section 2(13) of the Act. The dedication of the property by the founder of an endowment is obscure and no direct oral evidence is available, the Court will have to resolve the controversy about the character of the trust on documentary evidence, if any, the object and purpose for which the trust was created, the consistent manner in which the property has been dealt with or managed by those in charge, the manner in which it has long been used by the public, the contribution of the public, to all intents and purposes as a matter of right without the least interference or restriction from the temple authorities, to foster maintenance of the temple by way of grants from the state of gifts from outsiders inconsistent with the private nature of the trust, the nature of devolution of the property, are all important elements in determination of the question whether a property is a private or a public endowment. To sum up from the documentary and oral evidence produced, the following features are present in the present case: (1) The deity installed by the public was intended by him to be continuly worshipped by a indeterminating multitude of Hindu public: (2) In order to facilitate worship by the public the founder also intended that regular Bhajan, Kirtan and worship shall be maintained and annual ceremonies and processions for pilgrimage shall be conducted by the sishts in succession nomination nominated by the Reigning sist. (3) More than a century ago the temple in its own name was recipient of land by Royal grant and the same has been managed by the Saints in inheritance as Manager not as personal or private property.

The Income tax Officer issued a recovery certificate to the Additional Collector of Bombay against the petitioner under section 46(2) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922 for the recovery of the demand certified under section 46 of the Indian Incometax Act, 1922. The petitioner challenged the validity of the recovery certificate on the ground that the same offends article 22(1) and (2), article 21 and article 14 of the Constitution. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the income tax Officer issued the recovery certificate to a person who was not a defaulter of the Union and that the provisions of section 46(1) of the Act were not ultra vires article 14 of Constitution. Held, that the Income tax Officer was not competent to issue the recovery certificate under section 46 (2) of Indian Income tax, 1922, and the recovery of it being a Union demand there should be uniformity in the punishment to be meted out to defaulters and it could be done easily by suitably amending section 46(3) so as to provide for the detention of all defaulters for the same period in all cases in all States in all cases, in all cases. The object of the recovery of arrears of land revenue is one and the same, and it is levied under a single Central Act, and yet the ultimate coercive processes for recovery differ in nature and extent between State and State. The object sought to be achieved by the Indian Income Tax Act, 1879 became one and the different methods of recovery prevailing in other States could be devised by their own State, on a consideration of local needs, for the recovery, of their own public demands, cannot be regarded as bereft of a reasonable nexus or correlation between the basis of classification and the object sought to achieved by the Income tax Act any more than it can be so regarded with respect to the respective State laws.

The respondents were the trustees of the Port of Bombay. The Trustees, therefore, resolved that the shore crew at the Alexandra Docks should work for 8 hours and that there should be a variable recess of one hour and overtime of three hours should be paid. The Trustees accordingly resolved that the Shore crew at that Alexandra should work for 9 hours and that the shores should work for 10 hours and that they should work for 12 hours and that in case of an adult worker, whose minimum rate of wages is fixed under this Act by the hour, by the day or by such a longer wage period as may be prescribed, works on any day in excess of the number of hours constituting a normal working day, the employer shall pay him for every hour or for part of an hour so worked in excess at the overtime rate fixed under this section or under any law of the appropriate Government for the time being in force, whichever is higher. The respondents to this appeal were the trustees. The Trustees resolved that the workers at the Alex andra Docks must work for 8 hour and that there must be a variable decess of one and a half hours in any day and work up to 9 hours on any day can be taken without paying overtime if the total number of hours in the week does not exceed 48. The Trustees also resolved that the work of the shore shore crew should work for 7 hours and that it should be a fixed recess of two hours and overtime of two hours should be payable. The Trustees however resolved that the wore crew at 12 hours shifts should work for 3 hours and that this number was inclusive of one or more specified intervals. The Trustees thereafter resolved that the "neighbouring day" should be so arranged that inclusive of the intervals for rest in the work day of the workman shall not go beyond 12 hours. The Trustees then resolved that the wages of the shores shall be payable. On the other hand, the Act and the Rules fix the number of days of work, payment of overtime and for hours of rest in the worked day of the workmen. The Trustees further resolved that the workmen at the Alexander andra Dock should work for 4 hours and that no work shall be done beyond the 9 hours. The respondents filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the Act and also the Rules fixing the number of working hours, payment of extra wages and for hours and for hours for rest in their work day of work. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that section 13 fixes the number of hour in a normal workingday and that the number of workers which shall constitute a normal working Day shall be, together with intervals of rest over 12 hours, if any, it shall not spread over more than twelve hours on any particular day. HELD: (1) The scheme of the compels the inclusion of an hour of rest in a normal Working day is to specify that the interval for rest shall break up the hours of work. [901 D] (2) The expression "inclusive of one or two or more specified periods" in section 13 fixes a number of hours of work and hours of work (which cannot exceed 9) is part of the normal working day which may also include one or more specify intervals of rest. The words "inclusive of the intervals of rest" in section 14(1) are not intended to mean that the interval of rest shall break down the hours of the work.

The appellant landlord filed a suit for ejectment of the appellant tenant on the ground that the accommodation was let out on June 25, 1976. The accommodation was for the first time assessed for house tax by the Nagar Palika Ghaziabad with effect from October 1, 1976. On the date of the suit, the accommodation was for a period of 10 years. The accommodation had been let out on the basis of a notification issued under the East Punjab Act exempting buildings from the operation of the Act for five years and the view taken by this Court in Om 163 Prakash Gupta 's case was based on the language of Section 39 and 40 of the Act which is applicable to the present case. The appellant landlord filed an application for ejectment of his tenant on the grounds that apart from the controversy about the date which should be the starting point for computing the period of 10 year in view of the language of Sections 39 and 40, the provisions of this Act will be applicable to the appellant and therefore a decree for eviction could only be passed. The trial court decreed the suit. The High Court allowed the revision petition and decreed the suit for ejectment. The appellant tenant filed a revision petition before the High Court which allowed the revision and decreed the plaintiff suit for ejectment and directed the appellant tenant to be evicted. The High court allowed the revision application and decreed the appellant 's suit for ejectment on the ground of default in payment of rent. The appellant filed a revision before the High court which allowed the same and set aside the judgment and decree of the trial court. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The appellant landlord is entitled to the benefit of the provisions of Section 20 of the East Punjab Rent Restriction Act which became applicable to the premises in question during the pendency c.f the litigation. [167F] 1.2 The appellant landlord in the present case only seeks the protection of the new Rent Act which became available to him but looking to the language of section 39 of the Act it appears that the contention of the appellant could not be accepted. [167G] 1.3 The contention advanced by the learned counsel for the appellant was that because of the language in Section 39 and40 even if the matter is pending in this Court and 10 years have elapsed, the appellant will be entitled to the advantage of the Section even if the case is pending in the Court and 10 year have elapsed, appellant will be entitle to the benefit under this Act because according to him the appeal will be a continuation of the suit and therefore the advantage will be available. [167H] 1.4 The contention advanced on behalf of the appellant was not accepted as it is very clear from the language of this Section that it applied only to a suit pending on the date of commencement of the Act and this is the view taken in the Om 163 Prakash 's case wherein it was observed that if during the pendency of the proceedings 10 years have expired the restriction will not be attracted as the suit has been instituted within 10 years and therefore restriction as provided for in Section 20 will not be applicable and it is thus clear that during the pendency in this Court even of 10 years expired the restriction would not be attracted. [167D E] 1.5 The contention advanced was that because the language of the Section 39 and Section 40 even if the matters are pending in this court and 10 years had elapsed, the tenant will be entitled for the benefit of Section 20 even if the suit giving rise to the present appeal was pending in this High Court and 10 y years have elapsed.

The respondent landlord filed a suit for ejectment of the appellant tenant on the ground that the appellant was a thika tenant within the meaning of the Act as it was finally amended by an Act of 1953. The appellant contended that the respondent landlord was not liable to ejectment in the absence of any grounds therefor in the notice to quit in accordance with section 3 of the Act. The Subordinate Judge held that the appellant, Gaffur was not liable under section 3 of Act as it had been finally amended. The High Court dismissed the appeal. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the appellant had not established the existence of one of the grounds specified in section 3 of that Act as it stood before the commencement of the Act and that the definition of a thika tenancy in that Act was not such as to afford any protection to the appellant. HELD: (i) The provisions of the Act were prospective and as such inapplicable to pre Act suits, the landlord had to establish the existence of the one of the ground specified in section 4 in order to succeed. [723 C] (ii) The provisions in the Act were retrospective and as such applicable to pre Act cases, the landlord could not have filed a suit but apply to the controller for an order in that behalf. [724 D] (iii) The provisions were prospective and the landlord had not to file a suit but applied to the controller to pass an order in the matter. [725 E] (iv) The provisions contained in the Act of 1949 were prospective and they were inapplicable to pre existing suits, the landlords had to establish existence of one ground of the grounds mentioned in section 3 in order to entitle the landlord to eject a thika tenants after the Act had come into force.

The appellant was working as a Bench Secretaries Grade I in the State of Uttar Pradesh. He was promoted to the post of Bench Secretaries Grade II. He was later promoted to the said post. The pay scale of Bench Secretaries was revised to Rs.1600 2950 to Rs.2000 3050. The appellant was promoted to that post. The appellant challenged the said promotion before the High Court. The High Court held that it would be violative of the constitutional right of equal pay for equal work. The High court also held that it will be violative of Article 14 of the Constitution. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court had failed to appreciate the criterion provided under the Rules framed by the Chief Justice for the purpose of promotion to Bench Secretaries Grade 1 and that the High court had failed to take into consideration the criterion provided in the Rules framed in the matter. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The principle of "equal pay for equal Work" has to be construed in the first place. One cannot deny that often the difference is a matter of degree and that there is an element of value judgment by those who are charged with the administration in fixing the scales of pay and other conditions of service. If it has a rational nexus with the object to be sought for, as reiterated before a certain amount of value judgment judgment of the administrative authorities who are charged With fixing the pay scales has to be left with them and it cannot be interfered with by the Court unless it is demonstrated that either it is irrational or based on no basis or arrived mala fide either in law or in fact. [310C D] 2. The principle is of "equal work" and there is an ingredient of value judgment. [310D] 3. The classification made under the Rules, therefore, cannot be said to be violative of Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution of India. [310E] 4. The High Courts have completely overlooked the criterion provided by the Rules. The classification under the Rules cannot be said not to be violative Of the right to have equal pay for Equal work. [310F] 5. The High courts have completely overlooked that the principle of " equal pay for equality" has to been construed in the second place. One can deny that often, the difference is an matter of degree, and that there was an element of Value judgment by those whom are charged with fixing the pay scale and other conditions. If it had a rational nexus to the object to get, as reiterated in before a certain sum of value judgment of the Administrative Tribunal, which is being given to Superintendents or the Section Officers. The rules thus make a proper classification for the purpose o entitlement to higher pay scale. The classification is made under the rules, therefore, not violative of the right to get equal work.

The appellant was a tenant of certain lands in the State of Andhra Pradesh. The lease was for a period exceeding one year. The lease period was for a term exceeding one year and it was not enforceable against the Government. The lease expired on July 1, 1945. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the lease. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the words " such rights" in the third proviso to section 20(1) of the Abolition Act, were not intended to be super imposed on the right of the Government to terminate the lease. HELD: (i) The words " such right" in the second proviso are not intended to mean that rights created after July 1, 1944, are only voidable at the instance of the Government and that being the position, the Government must do some overt act to terminate the transaction. [557 D] (ii) The words 'such right ' in the third Proviso are not intended merely to include rights created after the 1st July, 1945, but also to include rights in any forest, mines or minerals, quarries, fisheries or ferries, the transaction must be deemed to be valid and enforceable by the Government against the person in whose favour such right had been created. [558 E] (iii) The words such rights ' in the second Proviso are not meant to be superimposed on the right created after July1, 1945, and the words "such rights" in section 20(2) must be construed in the light of the words used in the third provisos. [559 E] (iv) The words are not intended only to create rights created after August 1, 1945, are only permissive and not to create rights which are created after July. [566 F] (v) The words, " such right " in the third clause, are not intended either to create rights or to create rights in any land created by a landholder on or after July 1. 1945, but to include rights which are not created after July, 1, 1945 and to create rights, which are not existing before the notified date.
